The first half is on-the-ground reporting from Hot Chips and Semicon Taiwan; the second half is the real value of this episode: a bottom-up arithmetic of compute supply and demand, plus the judgment that anti-AI sentiment could swing elections.

3:05 The window for new AI chips has reopened
The author wrote last year that ‘the window for new AI chips has closed, except for Google's TPU’, and here he explicitly takes it back and says he was wrong. The trigger was OpenAI unveiling its in-house chip Jalapeno at Hot Chips, a short talk with high information density. Outside the hall a ring of new AI chip startups was gathered: Etched, MatX, Posetron, Fractile. Etched gave no talk but built presence by handing out hats while its founder peppered Q&A sessions with questions. The author reminds us these are hardware companies: they do not just design chips, they have to build their own racks and systems and get their hands dirty in the lab, and recruiting top talent and execution are hard barriers. His survival test borrows Nathan Bedford Forrest's controversial line: get there first, and with the most men.

6:08 Semicon Taiwan is really TSMC's request for proposal
First-timers are surprised: neither TSMC nor ASML has a booth. But TSMC dominates the whole show — its teams walk the hall visiting new suppliers and scouting new technology, and many information sessions are given by TSMC executives who lay the company's problems out in public. The author's conclusion is that Semicon Taiwan is essentially an RFP that TSMC issues to the entire semiconductor industry. The technical throughline is clear: future manufacturing has to go big. AI chips are hitting existing limits, most typically the reticle limit, which determines how large an area a lithography machine can print. TSMC had a slide showing a ‘battleship-class’ chip spanning 14 reticles that it plans to build, and the industry's response was, as usual, fast.

7:10 Glass panel packaging has moved from PPT to the show floor
Two years ago the author made a video on panel level packaging, which was the theme of Semicon Taiwan 2024, when it was still all talks and slideshows. Now AI systems are so large that the industry wants to use square, glass panel interposers to carry chiplets and memory in place of silicon interposers. The author is reserved: can TSMC make them without warping or cracking? ‘I'll believe it when I see the chip.’ But the ecosystem is already moving, and equipment such as handling robots adapted to square panels has appeared in the hall. He judges this wave of ‘chipmaxing’ will be one of the most far-reaching technology transitions in semiconductor history, roughly on the scale of the move to 300 mm wafers.

8:12 The spot market is gone, and VCs now hunt GPUs for their portfolio
When the author was last in the Bay Area in September 2025 the picture was completely different. Since then long-running agentic AI has swept Silicon Valley, triggered in part by stronger models such as Anthropic's Opus 4.5 around November 2025 and by Open Claw. Prices started rising in February 2026, everyone scrambled to lock up compute, and Anthropic led the way signing big deals with SpaceX, Google and others. The author was told that by the time of this trip the spot market had completely disappeared. For Neoclouds (a term coined by semi-analyst Dan Nishbal in April 2024 for pure cloud vendors that resell AI training and inference compute, such as Coreweave and Nebius) this is a huge boon, and they are certain the shortage will last at least another one to two years. The author met several people who did not know each other and each wanted to start a Neocloud. For AI startups this is a business risk: imagine telling investors your product has to wait until mid-2027 because there is not enough compute. The new way VCs help their portfolio companies is to go find compute, and he heard of people scraping together a thousand GPUs and even hunting in unexpected places like Eastern Europe.

9:12 Two giants are feasting while compute still goes to waste
By contrast, Anthropic and OpenAI are feasting internally. Dylan recently said on Dashpod that these two AI giants each have about 5 GW of compute. The author infers from this that a considerable share of all that compute may be wasted, and anecdotes he heard confirm that this ‘filthy rich’ supply is not being used as efficiently as it could be. He also asked every AI insider he talked to one question: will Google return to the frontier? The general consensus is no, though the explanations are vague. Several people pointed out that Google's decision to sell a large amount of compute to Anthropic is itself an admission that it does not believe. This is a big reversal from the period when Gemini 3 made some people think OpenAI was finished. What the author heard is that Google suffered severe talent drain, plus a culture unfriendly to frontier AI.

11:15 Neolabs are venture capital that treats compute as money
What fascinates the author most are Neolabs: research startups with basically no revenue that raise money to explore an interesting AI idea, whose founders are often elite researchers and whose business plan is little more than ‘discover a completely new architecture’. The most famous and earliest, Safe Superintelligence, raised a billion dollars and has yet to release a product or model. The label is fuzzy and covers recursive intelligence, Humans, Core Automation, Flapping Airplanes and others; those with products include Japan's Sakana AI, Thinking Machines, Reflection AI, plus a batch in verticals such as materials science, world models and robotics. The first reaction is that these assets are dumb: no revenue, no plan to monetize soon. But the author can understand it: historically breakthrough science came from research universities, government labs or Bell Labs, and now university funding is being cut and talent is being sucked into industry; AI is probably the first major technology in the past 50 years to emerge without government participation, and in this era research is closed and secretive. So let Nvidia, with its compute and cash, plus a pile of VCs, fund these asymmetric bets. OpenAI and Anthropic are locked into the transformer paradigm and are unlikely to spend on researching these directions. The probability of failure is high, but most of the money is given in the form of compute anyway; if someone really strikes gold and forces the giants to pivot (say, to a more data-efficient architecture), the giants will most likely buy the discoverer at an eye-watering price, and one such deal pays for everything. The author thinks this is a better use of cash than continuing buybacks, and names Apple.

14:15 Tokens are burning, and nobody has measured ROI
Customers really are burning tokens, but are they getting ROI? The author asked across the ecosystem and the answer remains vague: don't know, nobody has measured it, it is all anecdote. He believes lower barriers to coding will hit knowledge work — financial firms used to hire a pile of reporting analysts to keep management on top of positions, and now two smart young analysts plus Claude writing a dashboard is enough, which he has seen with his own eyes. But for other AI capabilities, such as making spreadsheets and making presentations, the things marketing usually pushes, he has seen no obvious impact. Maybe it just needs more time, maybe it is a problem of intelligence itself. OpenAI recently published a blog on how agents accelerate internal research, but still positions AI's capability as intern level: it can execute routine tasks, and is far from a real AI researcher. What he heard is that AI still lacks human research taste, though some believe sufficient scale can achieve it. And one thing holds for everyone in San Francisco: people are working harder than before. If the models are really that capable, why does everyone say they have more work? Maybe AI does not kill our work for us, but gives us more work.

15:17 Compute flips from shortage to glut in 2027
Everyone says shortage, shortage, two more years of shortage, and the author instead suspects things will not go as expected. His arithmetic is not complicated: usable AI data center capacity at the end of 2026 is estimated at about 15 GW, with OpenAI and Anthropic each taking about 5 GW; the supply chain will respond, and by the end of 2027 that number is estimated to reach 45-55 GW, an increment of 30-40 GW, of which the two giants take about 30 GW. Assume half goes to training, leaving 15 GW combined for inference. Inference is currently modeled at about $50 billion of revenue per gigawatt (a figure from Dylan Patel on Dashpod), and it can also be back-solved from Anthropic's deal to buy 300 MW from SpaceX for $1.25 billion a month; Dylan thinks smarter models can eventually push it to $100 billion per gigawatt. On that basis the two should produce $750 billion to $1.5 trillion of revenue in 2027. The author says that number is absurd: most people agree the two will do $150-200 billion this year, and he can barely imagine $400-500 billion next year, but $750 billion to $1.5 trillion is ‘two Walmarts’ or ‘two Toyotas’, a very strained credibility, and he does not think it will happen. He bets revenue per gigawatt comes in far below $100 billion or even $50 billion, possibly only a small fraction of it. The infrastructure side looks the same: assume 40 GW lands in 2027, current rent is about $20 million per megawatt, implying a 3-year payback, so those 40 GW require $800 billion paid to infrastructure providers, in 2027 alone. He does not think that can be collected either, which means rents have to fall and someone somewhere has to take a loss. Conclusion: in 2027 the supply chain will deliver a lot of compute, most of it in the second half, and he bets this pushes the market from shortage to glut. He stresses he is not saying the AI bubble will pop, only that we will soon be flooded with compute — 2026 is agentic demand matched against 2025 supply, supply will catch up and probably overshoot; but after that maybe the next phase of growth ignites and demand balloons again, for example persistent AI.

item.title: Stalin Was Just the Bookkeeper of the Revolution, and Then He Became General Secretary
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-empirehist-斯大林在革命里只是个管账的-后来却成了总书记/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-empirehist-斯大林在革命里只是个管账的-后来却成了总书记/
item.description: In 1917, while Lenin and Trotsky were on the streets calling for insurrection, Stalin was doing the organizing and fundraising nobody else wanted. He became General Secretary later not by oratory, but by sitting at the table.
item.content:encoded:
In 1917, while Lenin and Trotsky were on the streets calling for insurrection, Stalin was doing the organizing and fundraising nobody else wanted. He became General Secretary later not by oratory, but by sitting at the table.

This episode covers the groundwork before Stalin took power: Georgian origins, seminary, a failed bank robbery. Medium information density, but it makes clear why he was able to rise.

5:28 Even his birthday was something he changed himself
The parish register, the seminary certificate, the tsarist police files and his own handwritten questionnaire from the 1920s all say 18 December 1878. But the birthday he announced after taking power was 21 December 1879 — off by one year and three days. Bob Service offers one judgment in his biography: forgery was too easy for him. Service also has an unprovable but persuasive conjecture — that changing his birthday helped him dodge conscription when he was young. The thing itself is the theme of the whole episode: this man's attitude toward facts was instrumental.

6:35 How anomalous it was for a Georgian to become master of Moscow
His real name was Joseph Jugashvili, and he was born in Georgia. Georgia is in the Caucasus, next to Armenia, just north of Iran and Turkey, very far from Russia; it has its own language, its own alphabet, and its religion is Georgian Orthodoxy, which is not the same thing as Russian Orthodoxy. The analogy the episode gives is this: a man from a Georgian Orthodox background climbing to the top of power in Moscow is equivalent to a man from an Irish Catholic background, from some remote place like Limerick, becoming master of London in the mid-twentieth century. For Georgians at the time, being ruled from Moscow meant being colonized.

8:43 His father refused to change trades, and then started hitting people
His father Bessarion (nicknamed Besso) was a cobbler with his own workshop in Gori, and by most accounts a good craftsman. But he refused to keep up with the times: he kept making Georgian-style soft leather high boots while the market had already shifted to European shoes. He did not adapt; he became bitter, drank heavily, and the violence fell mainly on his wife Ekaterina (Kiki) and little Joseph, who was nicknamed "Crazy Besso." Stalin later told his daughter Svetlana a scene: his father was drunk and beating his mother, he grabbed a knife and threw it at his father, missed, his father charged, and he ran to a neighbor's house and hid there for several days until his father's rage passed.

11:52 Smallpox, a carriage, and a left arm that was too short
Around age six he caught smallpox, severe enough that his mother thought he would die — two older brothers had already died in infancy, and the family was too poor to afford a doctor, so they could only call a local folk healer. He survived, but his face was permanently scarred, and every official photograph was retouched. Later a runaway carriage hit him and broke his arm; the left arm never healed properly and was visibly shorter and stiffer for the rest of his life. The episode's formulation is: smallpox did not take him, his father's violence did not take him, and the carriage did not take him either. His mother was extremely devoted to him and had ambitious plans for him.

16:07 He wrote poetry, and he was good at it
Two things happened at once in his late teens: he began writing quite good poetry, and he entered the seminary. The episode reads one poem: "The pink buds have already opened, toward the pale violet violets; brushed by the breeze, the lily of the valley bends over the grass. Flowers, my Georgia. May peace come to my native land, and may you, friends, make our homeland famous through study." Anita says that in the original Georgian it is quite beautiful. It shows two things: he was a proud Georgian, not a Russian; and in the tsarist context, this way of writing about a "homeland" was already close to sedition.

19:09 The seminary was the tsar's Russification machine
In 1894 he won a place at the Tiflis Theological Seminary. The sign over the door said Georgian Orthodox, but the school was in fact under the control of the Russian Orthodox Church, one of the institutions the tsar used to "Russify" the borderlands. Students were kept under close surveillance, and reports were constantly written: are these people good tsarist subjects, are they talking sedition. And right under that surveillance, he was reading banned books, including What Is to Be Done? and other big questions about freedom and the individual. Anita's comment in the episode is: the surveillance here was not done well enough.

21:11 He gave himself the name of a bandit
On the banned list was a Georgian novel, The Patricide by Alexander Kazbegi, whose protagonist is a mountain outlaw named Koba. He took that name as his own alias, and his classmates at the seminary called him by it. The episode calls this a kind of "name determinism": he first took the name of a bandit hero, and then he really did become a bandit. The turning point from seminary student to bandit began when he saw with his own eyes two mountain bandits shot dead by police over a stray cow and publicly hanged in the center of Gori — he was forbidden to watch, but he went.

24:16 They stole 250,000 rubles and could not spend a single one
In 1907 he and a group of friends ambushed a bank carriage in Yerevan Square in Tiflis, almost within sight of the seminary: some stood on high ground throwing bombs down, others fired in the street, and the man organizing, financing and directing it all behind the scenes was Stalin, alias Koba. They got away with 250,000 rubles packed in linen sacks. But the bank had already published the serial numbers of its largest-denomination notes, so not one ruble of that money could be spent. It was the first time he left a police photograph on file, but he did not go to prison for it and essentially walked away untouched.

item.title: Outbound Reply Rate Near Zero? Don't Blame the Copy First — Check Who You're Sending To
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ycsp-外联回复率接近零-先别怪文案-先查你在发给谁/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ycsp-外联回复率接近零-先别怪文案-先查你在发给谁/
item.description: Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: get the person wrong and even perfect copy won't land. The debugging order a YC partner gives is — check the recipient first, then the company, then the subject line, and only then the copy.
item.content:encoded:
Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: get the person wrong and even perfect copy won't land. The debugging order a YC partner gives is — check the recipient first, then the company, then the subject line, and only then the copy.

Twelve minutes, eight tactics, high density but all immediately executable actions. For founders whose outbound reply rate is stuck in the single digits and who don't know what to change.

0:00 Send a hundred by hand first, then talk about automation
The most common founder mistake is opening a tool, blasting a thousand emails, and getting zero replies. The real loss isn't the zero replies themselves — it's that you learned nothing from them. The problem could be the copy, the company targeting, the lead filtering, deliverability, or the subject line, and you can't tell which. So the advice is to do at least a hundred outbound attempts manually before automating, and genuinely manually: spend time researching one specific person, what her problem is, what would grab her attention, read her LinkedIn and her company page. That homework, done yourself, is where high-converting outbound ideas come from.

1:04 Picking the right person matters far more than polishing copy
Founders often spend hours tweaking email wording while barely thinking about who they're sending to. Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: you have to find the person who has exactly the pain point you solve, otherwise even carefully polished copy won't land. A winter batch company selling an infrastructure product should have been selling to senior engineering leaders, but its actual list was full of dev rel managers, GTM managers, and even customer success managers — it sent hundreds of emails and naturally got no replies. Those wrong titles were never going to buy, regardless of how well the email was written.

2:06 Work backward from closed customers to the target title
How do you find the right title? Look at your existing customers first, then at the sales process: who pushed the last deal through, who signed the contract, who paid the money — list all their titles and go find people with similar profiles. You can also look at who has replied to your outbound. If you're still at the very earliest stage, with neither customers nor replies, ask yourself: who in the organization benefits most from buying your software. Example: selling employee device security monitoring software, the chief security officer might get fired in a data breach, so he'll be interested; an engineering manager would probably rather not be monitored, so he's not a good target.

3:09 List-building tools will hand you the wrong companies
Another common mistake is searching in Sales Navigator and getting back a pile of results that look like matches but are the wrong type of company — search tech companies, for instance, and you often get a bunch of IT implementation consultancies. So use list-building tools very carefully, and verify company by company whether it's really your customer. After doing a lot of outbound, you start noticing the clues that a company needs your product — intent signals. Job postings are a great thing to watch, since they reveal a company's priorities; company growth is another common signal: selling compensation planning software, companies under 100 people probably haven't introduced job levels yet, and companies over 500 have probably already set their comp bands, so crossing the 100-person mark is a great signal. Every product has signals like this; your job is to find your own.

4:09 Shake your network tree for the first customers
For closing your first few customers, starting from your personal network is much easier and converts at a much higher rate. Really shake the tree, make sure you cover everyone you know: first your personal network, then ask friends, family, investors, college roommates, people you met at a coffee shop for intros — literally anyone you can think of.

5:10 Executives don't care about your product features
The single most important thing in the email is clearly stating how you can help the other person. Figure out the three things that keep the buyer up at night: what gets him fired, what gets him promoted, and why he should believe you can help. When buyers read the email and think "this is exactly my problem," they're likely willing to take the call, even if they don't yet fully understand or trust your solution. The fact is executives don't care about your product features, don't care that your upload speed is blazing fast, and don't care that your database is written in rust — what they worry about is how to hit the quarterly target. Keep the product description to one sentence at most, and save the details for the first call.

6:14 A good email reads like a peer wrote it, not like a pitch
The email from the founder of Aptin, a YC company in the S24 batch, is held up as an example: the tone is very casual, it sounds like a peer, no jargon, no attempt to look impressive, like something a friend sent. He builds credibility with the first line — "I used to be a software engineer at Tesla. We got crazy good at using SMS to convert the people who visited our website into car buyers." The ending has a very clear call to action: would you be open to running an experiment to see whether AI can reactivate leads and lift conversion. The email also mentions that he noticed the phone number collected in the signup flow on their site, which makes it feel personalized; and the whole thing barely explains how the product works, only how it helps the other person solve a problem.

8:20 On LinkedIn, mutual connections is the top predictor
If email is about the subject line, LinkedIn is about your profile — it determines whether people accept your connection request and whether they reply. Key points: having a photo boosts trust; turn the top banner into company advertising that states clearly and concisely what the company does, avoiding jargon; rewrite the one-line headline and the about section into a short company description; move up what buyers care about (relevant and impressive experience, say) and cut the irrelevant — if the about section is full of hobbies and interests, it's harder for buyers to see how you can help them. Another place worth investing is mutual connections: the number of shared contacts is the single biggest predictor of whether someone accepts a connection request, so build up relevant mutual connections with your target audience — that takes time, and you should turn it into a habit of using your full connection quota every day.

item.title: World Models Are Not Video Generation: Atlas Makes 3D Control an Input
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-a16z-世界模型不是视频生成-atlas-把-3d-控制做成了输入/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-a16z-世界模型不是视频生成-atlas-把-3d-控制做成了输入/
item.description: Language models process tokens; world models process physical space. Atlas's key move isn't generating longer video — it's putting the camera and reference images into 3D coordinates as inputs, turning generation from a slot machine into directing.
item.content:encoded:
Language models process tokens; world models process physical space. Atlas's key move isn't generating longer video — it's putting the camera and reference images into 3D coordinates as inputs, turning generation from a slot machine into directing.

23 minutes, medium information density, but Justin draws the line between world models and video generation very clearly. Worth listening for anyone working in 3D, robotics, or VFX.

1:05 Atlas is a model release, not a product release
Justin clarifies right at the start: Atlas is not a product, it's World Labs's foundation model; products come later. It does three things — generate worlds that don't exist, reconstruct from real spaces, and simulate inside reconstructed spaces. Generation can start from text or an image, and then you can directly fly the camera through that world; reconstruction can take just one photo, or a hundred or more, and the more photos the more accurate the reconstruction; simulation is aimed at VFX and robotics. That ordering itself shows World Labs doesn't intend to build a consumer app first — it wants to stand up a horizontal foundation model first, then let products grow on top of it.

4:09 Reference images are pinned into 3D space, not fed to the model
Video models tend to drift and hallucinate their own direction after about ten seconds of generation. Justin says Atlas's answer is spatial context: the reference images you give it aren't ordinary images — they're grounded in 3D space, so you can specify ‘put this one here, that one there’. When generating video you're also not just giving a text prompt; you're directly operating the camera, telling it to fly in this direction or that one, achieving precise pixel-level control. So even if you generate for a minute, it's not pulling a slot machine — you are generating, directing, and controlling what the model outputs.

7:10 Atlas moves the 2D/3D fork earlier
Compared with Marble, World Labs's first product, Atlas is a completely rebuilt model stack. Marble put Gaussian splat at the center: video, 3D scenes, and mesh outputs all had to pass through a Gaussian representation first, then render back to images or video. Atlas breaks that dependency: the architecture is more unified and easier to scale, and the 2D/3D fork happens earlier. Generating 2D or video output is no longer bottlenecked on a Gaussian scene — the model gives 2D pixels directly; only in applications where you actually need 3D does it lift to 3D.

8:10 Gaussian isn't obsolete, it's just no longer mandatory
Justin doesn't think Gaussian has been outgrown — it's a tool, and you use it in the right place. VFX's final product is a 2D image or video, and may not need explicit 3D at all. But in real-time applications and on embedded devices, explicit 3D representations like Gaussian and mesh still have a place: in the future you might stream pixels in real time from a server farm, but we're not there yet, and it would be very expensive, so for client-side rendering, mobile, and VR devices, Gaussian or mesh is still useful. Its other role is plugging into existing workflows — people in games, VFX, design, and architecture already have pipelines built on 3D representations, and rather than making them switch to fully AI-native all at once, it's better to let AI enter their workflows.

11:13 Simulation covers the last stretch of robot training
On the value of real to sim for robots, Justin says the first thing is evaluation: a robot ultimately has to work in a specific factory, on a specific machine, in a specific environment, and you have to make sure it works in exactly that environment. So simulation is useful in the last stretch of training and evaluation — build a simulation as close as possible to the final use case, then either fine-tune a pretrained robot foundation model directly in that simulation, or run evaluations to confirm it works. That gives you a path different from ‘collect lots of demonstrations or human teleoperation’. He also describes a more aggressive version: take a few photos or casual videos with your phone, reconstruct the space with Atlas, describe the task in natural language, and let an agent build the simulation and do RL fine-tuning, getting a robot adapted to that space within minutes.

14:16 OpenAI dropping world models may be an innovator's dilemma
The host asks why OpenAI turned that Sora paper — ‘video generation models as world simulators’ — into a consumer product back then, and now isn't doing world models. Justin says he won't comment on OpenAI's internal strategy, but offers one explanation: there may be an innovator's dilemma — when you're holding something as strong as the LLM and leading in that direction, investing in the next thing isn't necessarily worth it. World Labs's judgment is that there's another class of model here, with a lot of opportunity, and they want to be the ones who seize it.

18:21 Three iPhones shoot bullet time, far better than expected
Asked about hard physics, Justin says he hasn't tried a black hole and guesses it wouldn't be too impressive. But what really surprised him was bullet time: three iPhones on tripods shooting in sync, then using Atlas to do a frozen-frame, orbit-around reframe. He cites the official example — a strawberry dropping into oat milk, time frozen at the instant the milk splashes up, flying a full circle around it, and the effect is completely insane. This capability needs only three input viewpoints. That shows Atlas's value isn't only in ‘generating new worlds’ — it's also in turning a small amount of real footage into shots that traditionally required a large camera array.

19:21 3D is underrated on the input side
Justin says 3D has value in two places. On the output side, everyone has already talked about it — sometimes you just need explicit 3D assets to drop into a workflow or game engine. But 3D's value on the input side is underrated: even if the final output is a 2D VFX shot, letting the model provide a 3D control surface helps the director decide what kind of scene the model should output. You don't want to write ‘push in, pull out, move left’ in text only — you want to grab the camera directly and have it zoom exactly the way you want, which text simply can't describe. So Atlas makes camera control a native input type: one of the modalities in the multimodal setup is the camera.

item.description: Deep sequencing shows that a few genomes in every thousand of a coronavirus population carry insertions, and a furin site has been hit independently at the same position at least three times — the probabilistic argument for a laboratory origin does not hold up.
item.content:encoded:
Deep sequencing shows that a few genomes in every thousand of a coronavirus population carry insertions, and a furin site has been hit independently at the same position at least three times — the probabilistic argument for a laboratory origin does not hold up.

The first half is the quantitative methodology of viral recombination and insertion; the second half is the real target of this episode: dismantling the laboratory-origin argument with numbers. Listeners who want the argument can jump straight to 52 minutes.

6:07 They changed the GFP sequence and the recombination rate went up
The team first built an OC43 reverse-genetics system and made a pair of viruses: each carried a frameshifted GFP, so infection alone produced only fragments, but coinfection followed by recombination could stitch green fluorescent protein back together. They expected that changing the nucleotide sequence of one of the GFPs would lower the recombination rate; instead it rose. Paul says there is only a hypothesis here, no data — one possibility is that after double-stranded RNA forms, the strand-transfer events of recombination become more likely because the duplex ‘breathes’. This counterintuitive result later became the reagent starting point for the whole paper.

11:12 Knock GFP out of frame and let insertions reveal themselves
Measuring insertions and deletions is far harder than measuring point mutations, because they were thought to be rare and sequencing depth was insufficient. Their approach was to put the GFP gene into the viral genome and deliberately knock it out of frame, preceded by a start-codon peptide that is in a different frame from GFP, so the virus does not glow green; it turns green only when that site acquires an insertion or deletion of a particular length that pulls GFP back into frame. This lets them count event frequencies and also pick out green viruses, read back the sequence, and infer the mechanism. This is where figure 1 of the paper comes from.

13:15 Knocking out NSP15 made insertions go down, not up
The original hypothesis came from prior work suggesting that NSP15, a nuclease, affects deletion rates — when you think nuclease, you naturally think deletions, not insertions. But the experiment went the opposite way: viruses with NSP15 showed a greatly increased rate of acquiring insertions that pulled GFP back into frame. Paul says the deletion rate could not be quantified this time because the numbers were insufficient, but the insertion result was black and white, and they were very surprised at the time; it was this accidental result that opened up the entire line of research.

22:26 Every base sequenced a million times before you dare talk about frequency
They moved from picking green viruses to brute-force sequencing: concentrating about 10 milliliters of virus down to 1 milliliter, loading part of it onto a sequencing chip, and producing hundreds of millions of reads, so that every nucleotide in the genome was sequenced at least a million times, with roughly 30 human genomes or 3 million viral genomes of data per virus stock. Paul stresses that depth has to match the number of virions in the sample — sequencing hundreds of millions of times when there are only a thousand virions in the tube is meaningless; they calibrated to sequence roughly a few percent of the viruses in the sample.

27:32 Eleven nucleotides is the threshold for judging origin
Short insertions (three to six nucleotides) can arise randomly in a viral genome, so their origin cannot be determined, and they were excluded from the analysis. They calculated that if an 11-nucleotide stretch matches the viral genome perfectly, the probability of that being pure chance is below 5%, so they restricted the analysis to insertions of 11 nucleotides or more. The result: more than 90% matched the viral genome perfectly or nearly perfectly, and in OC43 wild-type virus had 87 times more insertions than the NSP15 mutant, most of them derived from the positive strand.

36:41 Insertions are not rare events — they are a few per thousand
Vincent says that for years he was told insertions are rare, but the data suggest this has been happening all along. Paul responds that ‘rare’ is a relative term: one in a million is rare, but if you have ten million of them, it is common. The insertion frequency they give is a few genomes per thousand — roughly five to ten genomes carrying insertions out of a thousand virions. That frequency is lower than the point-mutation rate, but not by much. The reason it seemed rare in the past is that the vast majority of insertions are harmful or even lethal to the virus and are cleared at low multiplicity of infection, so they cannot be isolated.

55:05 Building a furin site is not hard at all
Mechanistically, a furin cleavage site needs at minimum two arginines, RXXR, and can even be cleaved with a single arginine plus other amino acids in support. Six of the 64 codons encode arginine, and multiplying the two fractions together, roughly 1% of random 12-base sequences encode an RXR motif. There are about 30,000 different positions in a coronavirus genome where an insertion mutation can occur. So this is not some enormous engineering challenge.

57:08 Lightning strikes the same spot at least three times
Putting the insertion frequency, the number of insertable sites, and the viral population size together, the probability of a furin cleavage site appearing at one particular position in a coronavirus genome is not astonishing, and it roughly matches what deep sequencing actually measured. In their deep-sequencing data, which did not cover the whole population, they had already found new furin cleavage sites independently at least three times at the exact position of SARS-CoV-2's existing furin site. Paul says the numbers in the paper are an underestimate: they focused PCR on just the spike region and required insertions to match the viral genome perfectly in order to rule out PCR artifacts, which very likely also excluded some naturally occurring sites that really exist.

item.title: Rome won with a crow: the key to the First Punic War

item.description: Rome turned sea battles into land battles with a boarding bridge called the corvus, cancelling Carthage's advantage in seamanship; but Carthage brought in a Spartan to rebuild its army and captured a Roman consul in return.
item.content:encoded:
Rome turned sea battles into land battles with a boarding bridge called the corvus, cancelling Carthage's advantage in seamanship; but Carthage brought in a Spartan to rebuild its army and captured a Roman consul in return.

This episode tells the First Punic War as a war history with mechanisms: the crow bridge, the sacred chickens, mercenaries, war elephants, all backed by concrete images and numbers, at high information density.

2:03 This was not a war between two equal powers
The host opens by calling this a clash of ‘the two great powers of the western Mediterranean’, and Eve MacDonald corrects him on the spot: at the war's outbreak Carthage was not necessarily a military power of that rank. Carthage had money, controlled the sea routes, and had centuries of alliance networks in western Sicily, but it had no strong standing army, relying on allies and mercenaries. What actually made Carthage a power able to fight Rome on equal terms was this war itself. So the story Roman sources tell over and over, of ‘Roman adaptability’, is only half the story; the other half is Carthaginian resilience and adaptability, without which there is no explaining why this war lasted more than twenty years.

15:29 Mercenaries at Messana dragged the two powers into war
The trigger was not the ambition of Rome or Carthage but a group of Campanian mercenaries called the Mamertines. They had seized Messana, and after being defeated by Hiero II, king of Syracuse, they split in two: one faction asked Carthage for help, the other asked Rome. Carthage acted from its nearby base in the Lipari Islands, and Rome then came too — and not as a small intervention, but as a full invasion with two consular armies. Eve points out that the Roman sources' claim of an ‘accidental empire’ is highly suspect, because the Romans showed up at Messana at the scale of an invading force. Polybius treats the Romans' first crossing of the sea into Sicily as the starting point of Roman imperial expansion.

28:14 The corvus turned a sea battle into a land battle
Carthage was a naval power, with skilled oarsmen and ships built fast and well; the Romans even built their warships to Carthaginian standards. But the Romans added one thing: the corvus, meaning ‘crow’, a boarding bridge that could hook an enemy ship. Once hooked, the Carthaginian ship could not move, and Roman marines simply crossed over and fought a land battle. At the Battle of Mylae the Carthaginians clearly did not expect this, and suffered heavy losses. Eve also cautions that the details of the corvus leave many unanswerable questions in the sources, but ancient historians all treated it as decisive. By the Battle of Cape Ecnomus the corvus was again credited as the chief factor, and Rome thereby opened the sea route for its invasion of Africa.

38:40 Carthage hired a Spartan to rebuild its army
After the Roman landing in Africa the Romans pushed forward, and it looked as though Carthage was finished. Carthage's response was to recruit a new army in the eastern Mediterranean and to bring in a Spartan commander, Xanthippus. He reorganised the Carthaginian army and reworked how the war elephants were used. Eve notes in particular that the Carthaginians had not used war elephants before; it was only after seeing the Indian elephants Pyrrhus brought that they realised they had a smaller African elephant of their own they could use. Xanthippus's reforms worked: the Roman army was destroyed and the consul Regulus was captured. This was Rome's first devastating defeat in the war, and it became a key event in later Roman memory defining the relationship between Rome and Carthage.

43:11 The captured consul went back to Rome to argue against peace
Carthage sent the captured consul Regulus back to Rome to negotiate peace. In the Senate Regulus said not to surrender, that Carthage was within reach. By agreement, if peace was not made, he had to return to Carthage and remain a prisoner. He went back, and died in captivity. Eve says the various horrific versions of how he died are not actually mentioned in the credible sources, so it is hard to judge how much is later embellishment; but what is certain is that he died in captivity in Carthage, peace was refused, and Rome kept fighting. This passage is a classic moment of Roman self-congratulatory rhetoric.

46:27 The sacred chickens would not eat, and the Roman fleet was finished
In 249 BC the Roman consul Tiberius Claudius Pulcher led a fleet against Carthage off Drepana. By Roman ritual, the sacred chickens on his ship had to eat for battle to be joined, otherwise it was a bad omen. The chickens would not eat, and he threw them into the sea, saying that if they would not eat, then let them drink. Roman sources present this as the most serious act of sacrilege, and the Roman fleet was then defeated at Drepana. Eve says that once Roman sources start emphasising a commander's arrogance and contempt for tradition, it usually means something bad happened. This defeat kept Rome from sending out a fleet for eight years.

50:48 Hannibal's father held Rome down with guerrilla war
After Drepana Rome vanished from the sea, and Carthage gained freedom of action on the western coast. In 247 BC Carthage sent a new commander, Hamilcar Barca — Hannibal's father. He brought a force Polybius calls the Mix-Hellenes, made up of soldiers of Greek, Libyan and Phoenician descent from North Africa, and fought a guerrilla war against Rome, occupying the high ground above Drepana and Panormus, with considerable success. Eve says this was the first time in the war that the Carthaginian army fought Rome this well. He also seized the temple complex at Eryx, dedicated to the goddess the Carthaginians called Astarte, and the two sides fought fiercely over this sacred site.

57:20 The rams from this war still lie on the seabed
The Battle of the Aegates Islands in 241 BC was the last battle. The Roman fleet hid behind the islands and ambushed a Carthaginian fleet heavy with supplies bound for Hamilcar. Eve says that if you go up to Eryx today, on a clear day you can see the Aegates Islands perfectly, and Hamilcar very likely watched this disaster unfold from land. More remarkably, the site of this sea battle has been preserved underwater: over the past twenty years underwater archaeologists have found large bronze rams on the seabed near the island of Levanzo, some inscribed with the names of Roman consuls, some bearing Punic inscriptions and carvings, along with Monte Fortino helmets and amphorae.

item.description: A Bunsen burner may actually increase settle-plate colonies in low-contamination environments; the cardiovascular benefit of vegetables may not run through the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway but through gut bacteria turning nitrate and iron into DNIC that directly activates sGC.
item.content:encoded:
A Bunsen burner may actually increase settle-plate colonies in low-contamination environments; the cardiovascular benefit of vegetables may not run through the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway but through gut bacteria turning nitrate and iron into DNIC that directly activates sGC.

The first half has clean experimental design and a counterintuitive conclusion; the second half's DNIC paper has a complete mechanism but dense terminology, suited to those willing to chew through mechanism.

6:05 A Bunsen burner does not reduce plate contamination
The authors used paired settle plates: one placed next to a lit Bunsen burner, one next to an unlit burner, both exposed simultaneously to the same contaminating airflow. The lit burner overall did not lower average contamination, and the statistical comparison showed no significant improvement. This directly challenges the common claim that there is a general sterile halo around the blue flame. The authors do not say the burner never helps, but that the effect depends on environmental conditions — they deliberately contaminated the lab air with Gordonia rubripertincta and then compared different flame sizes and dry versus wet particles.

10:13 83 CFU per minute is the crossover point
Under dry-particle conditions with an average 18 mm flame, they observed an apparent crossover point: when the airborne microbial concentration was above 83 CFU/minute, settle plates next to the Bunsen burner tended to show reduced deposition; below that level, deposition tended to increase instead. This can explain decades of contradictory anecdotal experience: people in dry environments genuinely believe the burner helps, while people in modern air-conditioned labs with low airborne contamination genuinely find the burner useless or even worse. Relative humidity in a typical modern air-conditioned lab is usually between 40% and 60%.

13:43 Airflow is not one-dimensional, so don't light a burner in a laminar flow hood
The traditional view is that convection pulls contaminants upward, but the authors point out that the same airflow may first drag contaminated air laterally across the work surface before it rises. Any upward airflow must be replenished from somewhere, so the most important thing during aseptic work is to limit wind or airflow. This leads to the most practical point in the episode: there is no reason to light a Bunsen burner in a laminar flow hood, since the flame itself disrupts the laminar flow. The authors did not directly visualize airflow; they measured a biologically relevant outcome — contamination — rather than fluid dynamics directly, and the authors themselves list this as a limitation.

17:49 Flaming tube mouths and lighting burners are both ritual
The authors compare this historically with the old practice of flaming culture tube mouths. Michael's graduate advisor at the time said stop doing it, there is no evidence it helps, and produced the 1972 paper proving it. The judgment in the episode is that changing behavior is hard, especially when ritual gives people a sense of control — lighting the burner feels proactive, flaming the tube mouth feels like protecting the culture, but there is no evidence it actually does anything. The authors do not argue for abandoning the Bunsen burner; they argue for measuring: use simple settle plates to measure your own lab's environment and let evidence guide practice.

28:14 Vegetables may protect the heart via the DNIC pathway
This Cell paper proposes reframing the entire nitric oxide synthase pathway: not a local paracrine model (eNOS makes NO that acts on adjacent smooth muscle), but an endocrine-like circuit — nitric oxide synthase makes nitrate, nitrate enters the gut, microbes turn it into dinitrosyl iron compounds (DNIC), which then act on targets such as the heart. If it holds up, the cardiovascular benefits of dietary nitrate (leafy greens, beets) may be mediated mainly by microbe-generated DNIC, rather than the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway we currently assume. The author is Andrei Kleshioff at the Karolinska Institute.

31:32 No DNIC can be found in germ-free mice
They used electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) to directly detect DNIC in tissues. Signals were visible in the liver and kidneys of healthy mice, but when the same detection was done in germ-free mice, no DNIC at all could be found in the tissues — the first hint that microbes are making it. After feeding inorganic nitrate, liver DNIC levels rose in conventional mice but not in germ-free mice; if ferric citrate was added to the nitrate drinking water, the liver DNIC signal rose even higher, while ferric citrate alone had no effect. The same in vitro: mouse and human feces plus nitrate plus iron can produce DNIC, while germ-free mouse feces cannot.

39:55 DNIC directly activates sGC, not via free NO
They used isolated mouse aortic rings, pre-contracted with phenylephrine, then added DNIC. To distinguish free NO from direct sGC activation, they used two pharmacological tools: one that scavenges free NO, and one that directly blocks sGC. The sGC blocker completely abolished DNIC-induced relaxation, while the free-NO scavenger only partially attenuated it. The conclusion is that DNIC activates sGC, but not through free NO — the FeNO2 entity itself appears to directly activate sGC. The same holds for bacteria-generated DNIC: only wild-type E. coli supernatant (anaerobic, with nitrate and iron) relaxed aortic rings, while a mutant lacking nitrate reductase did not.

47:16 DNIC suppresses leucine uptake and holds down mTORC1
On the metabolic side, they measured the phosphorylation state of key proteins in the liver mTORC1 pathway. In disease-model mice, mTORC1 was overactivated, downstream S6K1 phosphorylation was elevated, and transcription factors driving lipid synthesis were also elevated. Both DNIC treatment and nitrate-plus-iron supplementation brought these markers back to control levels. Mechanistically, they used glioblastoma cells to measure radiolabeled leucine uptake and found that DNIC inhibits leucine uptake in a concentration-dependent manner, suggesting it inhibits the leucine transporter — leucine is the key signal telling mTORC1 that nutrients are available, so blocking uptake blocks mTORC1 activation.

item.description: Private credit has poured into insurance companies, much of it in affiliated investments, rated by private agencies that are systematically too generous; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400-500 billion of capital a year.
item.content:encoded:
Private credit has poured into insurance companies, much of it in affiliated investments, rated by private agencies that are systematically too generous; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400-500 billion of capital a year.

The first half is industry lore; the specific mechanisms and numbers on private credit ratings, private equity in 401ks, and Social Security reform in the middle and back half are the part actually worth your time.

5:08 A stock fund should be 80-90% stocks
When Bob Posen took over as Fidelity's president in 1995, the firm was in an awkward spot: Jeff Vinick had moved half of the Magellan fund into cash, which both dragged on performance and violated holders' expectations of a stock fund. His approach was to build internal consensus first — if you run a stock fund, you must keep 80% to 90% of the position in the kind of stocks the fund's name implies; if you want balanced, if you want a money market fund, the firm has other products. His logic: investors bought this fund's stated positioning, and a manager cannot change that positioning just because he thinks "now is not a good time to buy stocks." That rule later became basic discipline for Fidelity's stock funds.

8:12 After assets double, split into small teams to keep the startup feel
Under Posen, Fidelity's assets under management grew from $500 billion to $1 trillion. His judgment was that the key to managing that much money is not process but how to preserve entrepreneurial spirit and a sense of belonging. The method was to split the investment team into a number of relatively small groups — value, growth, small cap, international — so each group had a stronger sense of ownership over results. At the same time he consolidated money market and bond funds in New Hampshire, because fixed income and money funds look at the same credits, and here scale is a friend that spreads out enormous economies of scale; stock funds are exactly the opposite.

19:21 Put private equity in 401ks, but cap it at 10-20% first
Posen is reserved about putting private equity into 401ks. The core problem is liquidity: if a participant puts all of their retirement assets into a single private equity fund, they simply cannot get the money out when hit with a medical emergency or when they reach the age for required minimum distributions. His proposal is that private equity can only be part of an asset-allocation fund or a target-date fund, not a standalone option; if it must be a standalone option, employers should set a cap, and the magnitude he gives is 10% to 20%. He draws an analogy to employer stock: GE employees who put their whole 401k into GE stock did not end up well, and a retirement account needs diversification.

21:25 The instant markup in secondary trades is an accounting loophole
Private equity is hard to value to begin with, and what worries Posen most is secondary trades: a private fund, needing to raise cash or nearing the end of its investment period, sells part of its portfolio at a discount to another private fund. There is a technical loophole in the accounting rules that lets the buyer immediately mark that investment up to par on its books even though it bought in at, say, a 5% discount. He thinks that rule has to change. Valuation is already hard enough; this kind of "instant markup" should not be allowed to lift book value out of thin air and pass it through NAV to holders.

24:28 Private ratings systematically overstate private credit
The private credit held by insurance companies can reach as much as $2 trillion on some measures, and a large share of it is "affiliated investments" — starting with Apollo, more and more private equity firms have become owners of insurance companies and then put debt related to themselves into their own insurers. Posen and his co-authors found that a great deal of private credit is rated by private rating agencies, and that rating shopping exists. Two studies, from Columbia and Imperial College, show these private ratings are systematically too high; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400 billion to $500 billion of capital a year. His fix is direct: make the private ratings public and let the market pick apart the assumptions and methodology.

29:35 Mark Walter's $20 billion of affiliated credit is a wake-up call
Posen treats the Mark Walter case as a wake-up call. Walter founded Guggenheim and figured out early that buying a life insurer lets you steer what was a conservative insurance portfolio into higher-yielding securities, including private credit related to Guggenheim or to its own portfolio companies. The rules themselves allow insurers to invest in affiliated private credit, provided it is disclosed to regulators. Regulators have now found that insurers controlled by Walter or Guggenheim hold about $20 billion of affiliated private credit, some of which may have been used to buy the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Lakers. Walter's side is trying to divest part of that affiliated credit. Posen stresses this is not just Guggenheim: large private funds including Apollo and KKR have all discovered that insurance companies are handy investment vehicles.

41:52 Someone with $1 million investable should not hold 40% bonds
Posen points out that most target-date funds arrive at retirement at 80% bonds and cash, 20% stocks, which is reasonable for people who have to live off their retirement portfolio. But more than 7 million Americans have investable assets (excluding their primary home) above $1 million; they do not live off investment income and can ride out a down year in stocks. He calculates that over a 30-year horizon, a 60/40 portfolio and the 90/10 he advocates (90% stocks, 10% cash) differ by a factor of two in terminal value — $5 million versus $2.5 million. He rebuts the objections one by one: over the past 60 years bonds only acted as a hedge in 10 of them; in 2022 stocks and bonds both fell about 18%; stocks fall hard, but look out two years, five years — after 2008, 2002 and 1974 they recovered and then some.

50:09 Semiannual reports are fine, but don't kill the Q1 and Q3 filings
Posen supports keeping quarterly reporting and opposes moving to semiannual. The reason is that the economy, diplomacy and companies' own circumstances all change fast, and six months is a long time; and the information vacuum created by semiannual reporting encourages insider trading. His compromise: at mid-year and year-end, file full 10-Qs and 10-Ks; for the first and third quarters, file a slimmed-down report, three or four pages plus the income statement and balance sheet — not a heavy burden. He rebuts the claim that "less reporting encourages long-termism": when the UK made the move from quarterly to semiannual reporting optional in 2013-14, he and a quantitative accounting scholar at Columbia compared the two groups of companies, and the ones that switched to semiannual did not invest more in R&D or capital expenditure.

item.title: Humans Spent Millennia Fighting Stank, and Perfume Started as Smoke for the Gods
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-extracredits-人类几千年对抗恶臭-香水最初是烧给神的烟/
