item.description: Perfume didn't begin as luxury or pleasure — it began as religious incense and disease prevention. Europeans believed foul air spread illness, so they walled themselves in with scent.
item.content:encoded:
Perfume didn't begin as luxury or pleasure — it began as religious incense and disease prevention. Europeans believed foul air spread illness, so they walled themselves in with scent.

Medium information density, but it strings together perfume's religious origins, the plague and the decline of bathing, and the transformation of Grasse, France into one continuous line — good for anyone interested in the history of the senses and the history of consumption.

0:02 Ambergris comes from a battle inside a whale
The episode opens with a very concrete image to explain where ambergris comes from: a sperm whale swallows a giant squid, the squid's hard beak lodges in the whale's intestine, gets coated in a mysterious bile secretion and expelled, then drifts in ocean currents for decades before washing ashore. Apothecaries buy it at the price of gold, grind it into a fixative, and use it to control how fast a scent evaporates, so the fragrance slowly changes over a whole day. The image shows how absurdly long the raw-material chain of perfume can be — behind a single scent lies a deep-sea struggle and decades of drifting on the currents.

2:04 Smell is the most emotional sense
The episode offers a judgment: by some measures, smell is the most emotional sense, because it connects directly to the brain's memory center. Research shows that recalling a smell evokes memory more strongly than visualizing does. Host Rob says his earliest memory is grabbing the rope seat of a lounge chair on Oahu's North Shore while learning to walk — what he remembers isn't the image but the smell of that old rope fiber soaked in sea-salt air. The other host's earliest olfactory memory is the old 1980s-formula Trix cereal. Smell can offend, can bring pleasure, can summon the past like a ghost, and is by nature untouchable, changeable, and fleeting.

3:04 The earliest perfume was smoke burned for the gods
Ancient perfume's origins were mainly religious, and it wasn't today's distilled liquid — the earliest form was basically smoke produced by burning. Egyptian priests burned specific woods, plants and resins to make pleasing smoke that both purified the ritual space and served as a channel for connecting with the gods. The word perfume comes from the Latin perfumum, meaning "through smoke." In China, Southeast Asia and Native American communities alike, these fragrances were believed to carry prayers and pleas up to heaven or the spirit world. In Asia this grew into an incense-making tradition that largely replaced personal perfume until modern times, because the scent would linger in clothing and rooms.

7:07 Ibn Sina invented steam distillation
In the 11th century the Arab scholar Ibn Sina discovered steam distillation: boiling a solid substance in water, collecting the steam, and separating the oil or essence from it. The first things extracted this way were rose water and rose oil, still a mainstay of cosmetic perfumery today. Like many chemical, scientific and mathematical concepts, the method passed in the Middle Ages from Arab to European scholars, and then to Italy, which became the center of European perfume-making throughout the Renaissance. The people making perfume then were often alchemists and apothecaries, and the perfumes they made were both drunk as medicine and worn on the body.

8:08 Scent was treated as an airborne barrier against disease
Before germ theory, European medical thought rested on miasma theory: foul or bad-smelling air was the main route by which disease spread. In an age without science this wasn't absurd, because rotting flesh, industrial burning and contaminated water really did make people sick. So Europeans concluded that inhaling sweet or pleasant-smelling air could ward off illness. The upper classes began using nosegays (a small bunch of dried flowers or herbs, held up to the nose when passing bad smells), gentleman's canes topped with a container of aromatic material, and perfumes worn, drunk or used to fumigate clothing as protection. Most famous is the plague doctor's mask, its hooked bird beak stuffed with flowers, spices and herbs.

9:08 The Black Death killed the public bathhouse
The Black Death may be the single biggest factor in Europe's adoption of perfume. The plague that swept Europe for three centuries killed off the public baths left over from the Roman Empire, because people believed water was a vector of infection. Moral norms then shifted, religious concern about public nudity grew, and bathhouses came to be seen as places for trysts or sex work. People switched to cleaning their hands and faces with damp cloths, and soaking baths became increasingly rare. They began wearing more undergarments to absorb sweat and odor so those could be changed and washed. In this environment, not just the upper class but the emerging middle class relied more on perfume, often making it at home from rosemary in the garden or alcohol plus purchased ingredients.

10:09 Scented gloves set off a political scandal
In the 16th century people usually scented their clothing rather than their bodies, and scented gloves, handkerchiefs and fans were especially popular. The French queen Catherine de Medici brought Italian perfumery traditions to the French court and hired the Italian perfumer Renato Bianco (Master Rene) to blend exclusive scents for her. Legend has it that Master Rene had a secret tunnel connecting his residence to Catherine's bedroom, and that he also served as her poisoner. When Catherine's rival, Jeanne III of Navarre, died after receiving a pair of scented gloves as a gift from Catherine, rumors spread that the gloves had been soaked in poison. Whether the poisoned gloves were real or not, several deaths were reportedly attributed to them, to the point that William Cecil advised the perfume-loving Elizabeth I to refuse any gift of scented clothing.

12:09 Grasse shifted from leather tanning to perfume
Catherine de Medici's passion for perfume changed the industry forever. The French city of Grasse realized the flower fields around it made it an ideal place for fragrance manufacturing, and with Catherine's support shifted its economic base from leather tanning to perfume-making; the city, and the country as a whole, remains the center of world perfume manufacturing to this day. France began to dominate the spice trade, and the French empire could bring in novel, far-flung raw materials from the Caribbean, Indonesia, India and China. French perfumers also created the language we use to describe perfume, and the three stages of a fragrance's evolution: top notes or head notes smelled in the first few minutes, middle notes that can last for hours, and base notes smelled in the evening or the next day. This evolution comes from fixatives controlling evaporation speed, such as ambergris or alcohol, revealing layers of scent over time.

item.title: Astra crosses the AGI threshold, but no one can audit it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-cogrev-astra-跨过-agi-门槛-但没人能审计它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-cogrev-astra-跨过-agi-门槛-但没人能审计它/
item.description: Astra frees humans from ever having to do certain tasks again, yet OpenAI paused only half its RL compute; external audit gets stuck two or three days before release, and there is no adult in the room to take the blame.
item.content:encoded:
Astra frees humans from ever having to do certain tasks again, yet OpenAI paused only half its RL compute; external audit gets stuck two or three days before release, and there is no adult in the room to take the blame.

The two hosts chain together the evidence for Astra's capabilities, the true magnitude of OpenAI's pause announcement, why auditing can't get off the ground, and why doomers can't hedge by shorting — high information density.

3:30 Astra holds long tasks together with a single notes file
In the past, models handling long tasks compressed a million tokens into a summary and opened a new window, losing all the detail. Astra instead maintains a long-lived notes file that the model updates at any time and carries forward with it, no matter how many tokens have already been written, and it can also search back through its own session history. So the same million-token context window can effectively manage roughly ten times that much context within a single rollout. Nathan calls this a mechanism that is "obvious in hindsight but genuinely new."

6:19 OpenAI self-reports 3.1 agent workdays per workday
In its research-acceleration blog post, OpenAI gives its own unit of measure, the "agent workday," reporting that each human workday corresponds to 3.1 agent workdays. Nathan admits the methodology is unclear; his reading is the literal one: for every eight-hour shift a human researcher puts in, the agent runs twenty-four hours in real time. The same post also has a chart grouping by human time spent and looking at Astra's success rate, effectively a substitute for the METR curve. Nathan says the METR curve hasn't been updated in a long time — not for lack of wanting to, but because the tasks aren't big enough anymore: the model iteration cycle is now shorter than the task length that needs measuring.

21:03 External audit is structurally stuck at two or three days
Prakash breaks down why external audit can't get off the ground: there are a hundred candidates in a model's lifecycle, and the release version is only settled in the last two or three days, so external auditors get only a few days. Bringing the audit team into the company a month early runs into a second layer of problems — audit firms are short on people and money, depend on funding from model companies, and their staff keep flowing to model companies; and if two companies agreed not to poach from audit firms, that would itself be an antitrust problem. He says the revolving-door problem in financial regulation remains unsolved to this day.

31:12 What was announced as a pause actually stopped only half
Nathan reads OpenAI's RL compute chart: what was announced was a "frontier scale RL pause," but in reality, when the Hugging Face incident was disclosed, half was stopped first and the other half kept running — and that half was already enough for the Astra model to take over part of OpenAI's research infrastructure; even so, it wasn't fully stopped, only half was cut. As for whether the remaining blue compute labeled "non Astra" contains a model stronger than Astra, he says he doesn't know, but "I've been disappointed before." Prakash adds: the real frontier model is not the one deployed, nor the one being trained, but the one in the researcher's head, because those ideas become models twelve to eighteen months later.

39:05 There is no adult in the room to take the blame
Prakash's rebuttal to Jacob Coxen's line that "accepting this race and entering the endgame is an arrogant gamble launched from a private company's Slack" is: then who do you want to hand it to? Pete Hegseth's Signal group? His judgment is that there is "no adult in the room" — there is no external savior, the whole world is held together with duct tape, and most of the smartest, most capable people to handle this are already inside these companies. Hand the decision to the government and what you get is political legitimacy, not wisdom, and not the legitimacy needed to execute. So the starting point has to be accepting that the world is just like this.

46:03 Operation Warp Speed is the precedent for a safe harbor
Nathan proposes the government should set a hard deadline the way you would with a child: you sort it out yourselves, here is the deadline, and if you can't, I come in and play the bad guy. The accompanying move is to first take away the antitrust excuse. Prakash counters with Operation Warp Speed: the pharma companies specifically demanded immunity from vaccine claims, wanted a safe harbor, and actually got legislation; without that exemption, they would have been sued into bankruptcy after the pandemic. So lawyers warning that "there will be retrospective reckoning in the future" is not alarmism — even if all current decision-makers agree, it doesn't matter, because the only thing that binds future decision-makers is law, not the verbal promises of today's people.

1:00:40 FSD's mistake is putting a human in the loop
Raffi has crashed a Tesla using FSD. His judgment is that FSD's interface design is bad, because it claims a human in the loop but when it actually hands control to the user, it gives nowhere near enough time to understand the situation and decide what to do; Waymo's design premise is that there is no human to take over, so the safety argument is entirely different. He personally would be willing to drive FSD again on the highway, or at least sit behind the wheel, but would be more hesitant on local streets in Palo Alto. The same company also has two kinds of code contracts: the Firefox team allows only humans to commit, while the Mozilla AI team has an entire codebase not a single human has written a line of — people only write the spec, and the whole codebase is automatically regenerated when CI builds.

1:29:15 The takeover is already complete, no one just admits it
The key disagreement between Prakash and Daniel: Daniel hasn't realized this has already happened. The financial market is itself a paper clipper, the means of production are the financial market, and the financial market is already fully fused with AI. Humanity took roughly a hundred years to hand full control of the means of production to the financial market. He says don't think of AI as a chat box; it is a global information process that need not run in a single box, and need not even be silicon-based — humans together with AI agents can constitute this information process. The reason Jacob became disillusioned is that he discovered in the Slack group that there was no control at all, yet he still assumed there existed somewhere in the world a group that could actually make decisions.

item.title: Enterprises will run 80% of tokens through open models, but spend only 20% of budget
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-ycsp-企业最终八成-token-走开源模型-但只花两成预算/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-ycsp-企业最终八成-token-走开源模型-但只花两成预算/
item.description: Open models and closed frontier models are not substitutes: the vast majority of tokens will run through open models, the hardest work stays with the frontier labs, and routing and orchestration connect the two in between.
item.content:encoded:
Open models and closed frontier models are not substitutes: the vast majority of tokens will run through open models, the hardest work stays with the frontier labs, and routing and orchestration connect the two in between.

The Ollama CEO brings first-hand token-flow data: local and cloud model mixes look nothing alike, and the real constraint on enterprise purchasing is security, not cost.

1:03 The driver behind open models is control, not saving money
Jeff says cost is the biggest pain point open models can solve immediately, but the enterprise north star is ‘better control over AI and customising it for yourself’. Cost is just the piece that can be solved in the short term; only once it is solved does customising the model to your own use case come up. The order matters: if you treat open models purely as a cost-cutting measure, you will misjudge why they are spreading so fast inside the Fortune 500. AT&T has already moved 40% of its token consumption onto open models, currently mostly US and European models, while also evaluating Chinese ones.

4:05 Two inflection points: coding agents, then OpenClaw
The per-user token usage curve on Ollama's cloud has two clear inflection points. The first came early in the year, driven by coding agents — Kimi, GLM and MiniMax launched in succession, and for the first time open models could carry a coding agent. The second came in April, brought by OpenClaw, as users expanded from developers to non-developers: finance, support, marketing and sales can all hand a hard problem to an open model and let it run to completion, picking tools and pulling data along the way, burning enormous numbers of tokens. Context windows growing from 128K to over a million is the technical precondition for this explosion.

8:08 Model launch day is a 24-hour fire drill
Ollama is a coordination channel for model vendors ahead of launch, but Jeff says getting a model a few weeks early counts as lucky; most of the work is crammed into the final 24 hours before release. Three things have to land at once: inference engine support (often weeks of work, and it has to be fast, accurate and consistent with the reference implementation), the accompanying harness (there are plenty of open-source harnesses now, like Codex and OpenCode), and capacity from hardware and inference providers — launch day is usually the single biggest day of growth. He compares it to an operating system: drivers, the inference layer and the application runtime all have to be glued together, and it is a combinatorial explosion problem.

14:11 The new scarcity sits above the token
Jeff cites three directions from Anthropic's platform team: knowledge (wiring company data and context into the model), coordination (one request spawns a pile of sub-agents, some in the cloud and some local, that need scheduling), and execution (sandboxes and compute). His judgement: tokens are already in oversupply, dozens of open model providers can supply them, and what is scarce is how to orchestrate an agent from A to B above the token. Following the path of cloud computing, developers ultimately prefer the best standalone product at every layer rather than something bundled together like Heroku or Google App Engine.

17:14 Stateful things will not sink into the model layer
Asked whether harnesses will be absorbed by the model, Jeff's judgement is that the core loop and hooks will sink into the model, but a few categories cannot. One is the state problem — models are trained on a monthly cadence and can never catch up with the latest data, so storage is a huge standalone problem space. The other is credential management and security. Open models do not come with a whole security toolchain the way closed providers do, and that is critical to enterprise adoption. This explains why the stronger the models get, the more middle layers there are.

18:15 80% of tokens run open, but only 20% of budget
Jeff's steady-state judgement: the vast majority of tokens inside an enterprise — his figure is 80% to 90% — will run through open models, but that does not mean 80% to 90% of budget goes to open source. The open community is driving cost extremely low, so maybe only 10% to 20% of spend lands on open models. The hardest work stays with the frontier labs, because that is where the best researchers are; the big middle is open and closed combined. He uses a law firm as the analogy: the partner hands work down to a pile of associates.

22:19 Local and cloud model mixes are not remotely the same
On local models, US and Chinese models are roughly neck and neck; on cloud-hosted models, it is almost entirely Chinese models. Jeff says local is a three-way mix of US, European and Chinese, while cloud coding agents are dominated by Chinese models. The division of use cases is clear too: coding agents write code and tests, hit many hard problems, and mostly rely on large cloud models; workflows with low end-to-end difficulty like document processing run very well locally. So it is a hybrid execution model — simple tasks run locally, plus a router deciding when to go up to a large model.

29:25 The Flash tier is the precondition for unlimited tokens
Jeff says that early in the year open models had just caught up to the intelligence frontier, within less than 3 months of the closed frontier, and the next problem to solve was extreme efficiency. The key metric for models like DeepSeek Flash is not just low cost per token but low cost per task. These models are good enough for 80% of tasks, fast and extremely cheap, and will become the workhorse doing the grunt work. He recalls that in the ChatGPT era nobody thought about token usage, and we will eventually return to that state, but it requires model architectures trained specifically for high token volumes. The fastest-growing segment on Ollama's cloud is precisely the DeepSeek line, driven mainly by Flash adoption.

item.title: One Report Closed Over a Hundred Medical Schools, and Black Doctors Were Cut Off for Decades
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-stuffmissed-一份报告关掉上百所医学院-黑人医生从此断层/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-stuffmissed-一份报告关掉上百所医学院-黑人医生从此断层/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: The Flexner Report is often written up as the starting point of modern medical education, but it also closed five of seven Black medical schools, and nearly forty years passed before another Black medical school appeared.
item.content:encoded:
The Flexner Report is often written up as the starting point of modern medical education, but it also closed five of seven Black medical schools, and nearly forty years passed before another Black medical school appeared.

Medium information density. The first half is a chronological slog through Flexner's life; the real value is in the second half, on how the report reshaped medical education and how it cut off the supply of Black doctors.

6:09 The report's author was not a doctor but an education reformer
Abraham Flexner was not a medical man. In 1890 he ran an experimental school with no fixed curriculum, no exams and no grades, and its students still got into good schools; in 1908 he wrote The American College, A Criticism, attacking American higher education, which is why Henry Smith Pritchett of the Carnegie Foundation came to him and asked him to turn the same critical eye on the medical schools of the United States and Canada. He spent two years travelling to 155 medical schools, recording each one's admission requirements, faculty, finances, laboratories and hospital affiliations, and in 1910 delivered Medical Education in the United States and Canada. It was precisely because he was an outsider rather than a member of the medical community that the assessment dared to be so unsparing.

14:23 Medical schools were still teaching out-of-date knowledge
In the fifty years before the report, bacteriology, diagnostic technique and surgery were all changing fast, but medical schools had no uniform standards. At many schools the faculty were practising physicians who taught the way they themselves had been taught and did not update the content. The result was that the care the doctors they produced gave patients was, at best, antiquated and, at worst, life-threatening. Admission standards were just as chaotic: when the report was published, 74% of medical schools required only a high school diploma, some accepted even a high school equivalency certificate, only one in five required more than two years of college coursework, and many schools were essentially for-profit businesses.

18:31 He recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools
Flexner set standards first and then scored school by school: admission should require college-level biology, chemistry and physics; the curriculum should include classroom and laboratory work in anatomy, pathology, bacteriology and pharmacology; there should be a teaching hospital for hands-on practice; and teachers should be salaried, full-time teaching and research staff rather than practising physicians moonlighting as instructors. He published the results by state and by school, naming dirty laboratories and lax standards, and criticising course schedules that left students sitting for hours, exhausted, listening to dull lectures by part-time teachers. In the end he recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools. Within a decade the number of American medical schools was down to half, the surviving schools reformed their standards and curricula, and laboratory and clinical teaching were modernised on a large scale. In Canada only one school made the closure list, and it ultimately did not close.

23:43 He never did the books on Black medical schools
The report was equally unsparing toward Black medical schools, writing that five of the seven "can make no valuable contribution at this moment", and endorsing only Howard and Meharry as worth developing. But the assessment did not take into account that Black medical schools charged far lower tuition than white schools, had smaller endowments, and were already running on extremely thin margins. He wrote that "the Negro needs good schools rather than many schools", and said that one of the most important duties of Black people and Black nurses was to teach hygiene rather than life-saving skills — a statement that is itself racist. Every Black medical school he named as inadequate closed: the first four shut before 1914, the fifth in 1915, and the last held on until 1923.

25:48 The next Black medical school had to wait until 1966
Howard and Meharry survived and are still there today. But the next medical school aimed primarily at Black students was Charles R. Drew Medical School in Los Angeles, which did not open until 1966 and was a response to the Black community's need for access to care; the one after that was Morehouse School of Medicine in Atlanta in 1975. The direct consequence of narrowing the options was a huge care gap: many potential doctors were shut out of educational opportunity by geography, and Black patients were often cared for by white doctors who, even at best, carried inherent racial bias. An expert panel convened by the AMA's Institute for Ethics in 2005 concluded that Flexner's line about "good schools rather than many schools" ensured that medicine remained segregated, and that the communities that most needed doctors were left without them.

26:51 The AMA was paying behind Carnegie's project
One fact not disclosed at the time: the Carnegie Foundation hired Flexner for the project, and the AMA was also a sponsor. There is also an unresolved question — whether someone connected to the AMA accompanied him on some of the school visits. He gave differing accounts at different times, sometimes saying the man went with him, later changing his story to say they merely met there, so whether the report was subject to more direct directional influence cannot be determined to this day.

28:53 Did he know he was constraining Black medicine?
He knew. The report contains a passage of idealistic colour, saying that building up Howard and Meharry would benefit the nation far more than barely sustaining more schools. In 1933 he wrote to the board of the institute he had founded, arguing that hiring and admissions "shall not directly or indirectly take race, religion or sex into consideration". One explanation comes from his biographer Thomas Neville Bonner: when Flexner was growing up in Louisville, the local Black community had more services and opportunities than in many places, with a dozen or so Black schools and vocational training in medicine and law for Black students; the Flexners were not well off, there were Black families among their neighbours, and he and his siblings often played with Black children in the community. This may have left him overly idealistic about the reality of Black family life, and he later admitted that it was not until he began studying educational institutions that he realised how disadvantaged those Black classmates of his had been.

35:01 The hygiene line may not have been his own
The claim that hygiene was the main duty of Black doctors is one of the key pieces of evidence for judging Flexner a racist. But the leaders of Meharry and Howard had said similar things in 1907 and 1908 — two or three years before the report — and those leaders were also white. This suggests Flexner's formulation may have been a restatement of the schools' established mission rather than a judgement he arrived at independently. In 2011 Lynn E. Miller and Richard M. Weiss, writing in the Journal of the History of Medicine and Allied Sciences, proposed another possibility: that this language was in fact opening up a public health role for the doctors at these schools, in order to win support across racial divides — because those statements about hygiene being the most urgent need were immediately followed by the conclusion that these institutions obviously ought to be supported. In 2008 the AMA issued a public apology for its history of racial inequality.

item.title: Change One Law of Physics and Every Wish Backfires
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-skeptics-改一条物理定律-每个愿望都会反噬/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-skeptics-改一条物理定律-每个愿望都会反噬/
item.category: The Skeptics' Guide to the Universe
item.description: A live thought experiment from Dragon Con: you may change exactly one law of physics to make science fiction real, and every wish gets taken apart for the consequences nobody counted — antigravity means free energy, hyperspace travel means handing the technology to every alien civilisation.
item.content:encoded:
A live thought experiment from Dragon Con: you may change exactly one law of physics to make science fiction real, and every wish gets taken apart for the consequences nobody counted — antigravity means free energy, hyperspace travel means handing the technology to every alien civilisation.

The first half is live riffing; the second half — the Roman telescope, robot babies, the falling-atom experiment on the Chinese space station and the Verne details — is denser and worth skipping ahead to.

2:07 Changing a law of physics changes it for the whole universe
The rules are hard: pick exactly one, and it must be practical and feasible within the laws of physics — no perpetual-motion-style having it both ways. Steven starts by sentencing most science-fiction premises to death — warp drive, shields, phasers, artificial gravity, antigravity — either they violate physics or they are non-trivial: theoretically maybe possible, but never going to happen. The real fun of the whole discussion is not in what you pick but in finding the consequences nobody counted inside each wish.

8:08 Antigravity is free energy picked up along the way
Jay wants antigravity, on the grounds that transport, construction and materials handling would all change. Bob points out it is a twofer: if you could feasibly switch gravity off, you could turn gravity on while the water wheel goes down and off while it is lifted back up, and you have a perpetual motion machine. Steven, as buzzkill, patches it by force: the energy consumed switching gravity off must equal the energy you get out of it, no free lunch. The argument also sentences science-fiction movies to death along the way — single-stage-to-orbit is simply impossible in a 1g gravity well, and every shot of a ship reaching orbit in a minute is lying, because it assumes antigravity exists.

10:08 Hyperspace travel hands the technology to every alien civilisation
Bob picks entering subspace/hyperspace: you travel there under an ordinary engine and come out having crossed a far greater distance — essentially practical FTL. He argues there is no downside risk, because hyperspace is separate from real space and does not affect our universe. Steven and Jay immediately counter: changing a law of physics changes it for the whole universe, not just for you, and hostile civilisations could use it to colonise Earth just as well. Bob's answer is to hide — human radio signals dilute into noise a few light years out, so in principle Earth's life cannot be inferred from them. Jay offers a compromise, jump gates: both ends have to be built, so expansion can only be slow, and not every alien will come knocking.

23:16 Zero-point energy is too thin, and forcing it triggers a big rip
Steven's second choice is free energy, specifically zero-point energy. Bob gives the objection: zero-point energy is observationally extremely thin, and lighting a single bulb might require several cubic light years of space; and if you really injected that much energy into space, cosmic expansion would run away into a big rip that destroys all life. Steven's response is that this is exactly why these are not laws of physics — every wish, once it actually lands, brings catastrophic consequences, so the fun of the thought experiment is finding the loophole that dismantles the wish. Julia adds her astrophysics-major perspective: if gravity had a dial, 90% of the observations that infer stellar phenomena from gravity would all be ruined.

36:19 A bucket of water can compute like a neural network
The core of physical reservoir computing: any nonlinear system — a bucket of swirling water, time-varying mayonnaise — as long as you measure the right places, its nonlinear interactions can be mapped onto an artificial neural network and made to ‘think’ for you. Someone gave a talk saying ‘we made mayonnaise think very slowly’. Once that analogy holds, scale becomes a variable: if you had a nonlinear system the size of a nebula, you could feed it input and measure output at the right points, and it would do the computation for you. The speaker himself admits this is a ‘wild idea’, but stresses that once you shrink physical constants to something tiny, a pile of strange corollaries pops out.

44:29 Roman is a thousand times faster than Hubble, but cast as a supporting player
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is a wide-field infrared telescope with a 3.4-metre primary mirror, the same size as Hubble, but its design goal is not ‘better than existing telescopes’ — it is complementary: James Webb excels at deep space, Hubble at staring at specific objects, Roman at seeing a huge swath of sky at once. It can survey a thousand times faster than Hubble, and over its five-year mission it would sweep an area of sky equivalent to a thousand years of Hubble. Once it finds something interesting, Webb and Hubble can be turned to look closely. It will also build a three-dimensional map of the universe and carries a coronagraph to block starlight glare and directly image exoplanets — it can find smaller planets farther from their host stars, correcting the transit method's and radial velocity method's bias toward ‘hot Jupiters’.

55:41 A robot baby kicks its legs and kicks up explore versus exploit
The University of Hamburg and Czech Technical University did a ‘robot in a crib’: a baby robot, iCub, placed in a crib with a mobile carrying a QR code hanging above it, one leg tied to it by a string, and their own deep learning algorithm run to predict the mobile's motion. The result was that the algorithm spontaneously produced the explore versus exploit trade-off — both curious exploration and exploitation of the causality already learned. The researchers treat it as a platform: a baby's learning algorithm cannot be changed, but a robot's can, so different versions of contingent learning theory can be tested. By contrast, the mainstream of current robot control is deep reinforcement learning: put thousands of copies of the robot in simulation, train with a reward function, then transfer to the real machine in one shot — that is ‘do this and something good happens’, not ‘this causes that’.

1:04:44 The Chinese space station redid the Leaning Tower experiment with rubidium atoms
On the Chinese space station, researchers redid Galileo's falling-body experiment with two clouds of rubidium atoms of different isotopes, one heavier than the other. The free-fall time was about 10 to 12 seconds, far longer than in ground experiments, and averaging over many repeats, the two clouds fell at rates identical to five parts in ten million. What this verifies is that gravitational mass and inertial mass are exactly the same — in Newtonian mechanics mass shows up in two ways, and in free fall the two effects cancel precisely. What Einstein asked was exactly this: why must they be the same? There is no reason they must be. From that comes his thought experiment: in free fall gravity seems to vanish and you are in an inertial reference frame; and in an accelerating elevator light bends, so if gravity and acceleration are equivalent, gravity should bend light too.

item.title: Companies Are Becoming a Series of Nested Loops, but Loops Only Climb to a Local Optimum

item.description: After prompt comes agent, after agent comes loop. A loop will help you climb to a local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain.
item.content:encoded:
After prompt comes agent, after agent comes loop. A loop will help you climb to a local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain.

Anish strings together agent deployment, model pricing and the consumer AI bottleneck into one line, and the second half — on moats and product problems — is worth more than the first.

0:00 Nobody funds ideas that are too small anymore
Anish says that three years ago, if a company wanted to do something too grand, a16z would not invest; today it is the reverse — ideas that are too small, too local, they do not want to touch. The reason is that model capability has torn down the ‘can it be done’ threshold, and the remaining constraint is ambition itself. He calls this technology ‘unbundling skill from desire’: not only can productivity be amplified, the scale of what you want to do can be amplified too.

6:10 It is not recursive self-improvement, it is autocatalytic
Anish pushes back on the ‘fast takeoff’ narrative: the people who understand it best in the labs do not say RSI (recursive self-improvement), they say autocatalytic effects — using new technology to improve your own process, but not truly recursively. He gives two counterexamples: first, economic diffusion is extremely slow, and when he went back to his hometown he found people's lives had not changed much; second, many problems are simply not intelligence bound — give FedEx or Domino's a data center full of PhDs and it still will not let supply chains and pizza crush everything exponentially.

8:16 Using AI and reorganizing around AI are two different things
Anish uses the diffusion of electricity as an analogy: from the invention of electricity to factories actually reorganizing took 40 years, and it meant burning down the old plants and rebuilding, not swapping coal for electricity. Today the most aggressive companies redesign everything around models, while slower companies just grant permissions to existing roles and functions. He also cites the Mexican used-car company Kavak's Jedi Academy: a six-week course teaching everyone including mechanics to use the new tools, and at graduation each person delivers an agent in the production environment.

11:18 Companies will become a series of nested loops
Anish's steel man: after prompt comes agent (a loop of model plus tools, memory, skill files), after agent comes loop (a group of agents doing a task). Coding got there first because the models are best, the users are the most technical, and a mature loop already existed — bug report comes in, generate a reproduction, fix it, high-risk changes get human confirmation, low-risk ones ship directly, and it can even automatically reply to tell the customer. Above that there is loop per person, loop per job function, loops across business units, up to a loop that can run most of the company.

14:18 A loop only climbs to a local optimum and then stops
The growth team's version of the loop: every variant is generated automatically, measured automatically, and once it reaches statistical significance it converges and ships, with a long-term holdout left in place, and then the next experiment begins. But Anish stresses that a loop will hit a local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need out of distribution thinking and human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain. His example is telling Claude ‘make me a million dollars, no mistakes allowed’ — it cannot do it, because the direction has to be set by a human.

21:32 Frontier model pricing is actually irrational
Anish explains model choice with Pareto efficiency: frontier models are ‘irrationally priced’ on the price-performance curve — one more IQ point can cost 100 times more than Opus. But for industries with unbounded upside like drug discovery, that one extra IQ point might be worth a trillion-dollar outcome, so paying that price is rational; while for work with bounded upside like law and finance, you just want Pareto efficiency and a cheap, good-enough open-weight model. The conclusion is that the two architectures will coexist, not one or the other.

31:46 People want to spend time, not save time
Anish says ‘loop, make me happier’ is the big opportunity: people say they want to be more efficient, but in reality they want to spend time — the biggest products in the world are entertainment and social, not productivity tools. He distinguishes two kinds of users: the AI users on X fear falling into a permanent underclass and argue endlessly about whether GLM or Kimi is stronger; the Instagram user just thinks ‘this is a better Google search’. He thinks this is not a model or capability problem, it is a product design problem: for the past 40 years we built technology that extends the intellect, and we did not build things that extend the soul.

34:49 Consumer AI is still stuck in iPhone 2010
Anish compares the present to iPhone 2010 — Airbnb, WhatsApp and Uber had not appeared yet. Three things are holding back consumer: models are too expensive, so it is not easy to build a free product; the interface problem, chat only suits ‘the highest-agency people in the world’ like Elon and Sam, while the ideal interface for the ordinary consumer is TikTok, and you need to find something between chat and TikTok; and the technology has been too skewed toward productivity rather than human connection and entertainment. He thinks all three are now loosening: open-weight models have brought costs down a lot, founders like Eugenia are seriously thinking about interfaces, and Brian Chesky has also set up a lab focused on the next generation of interfaces.

item.title: Copper grades have fallen from 2% to 0.4%, while AI's power demand is going to the moon
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-oddlots-铜矿品位从2-跌到0-4-ai的电力需求却要上天/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-oddlots-铜矿品位从2-跌到0-4-ai的电力需求却要上天/
item.description: Global copper grades keep sliding, new mines take 35 years to permit, and an AI search uses 30x the power of a normal one — supply is shrinking, demand is exploding, and copper is becoming the new oil.
item.content:encoded:
Global copper grades keep sliding, new mines take 35 years to permit, and an AI search uses 30x the power of a normal one — supply is shrinking, demand is exploding, and copper is becoming the new oil.

Robert Friedland distills the copper supply-demand deadlock from 40 years in mining: falling grades, 8-year equipment lead times, sulfuric acid shortages. High information density, but the real goods only come in the back half.

14:30 The next 18 years will require digging up all the copper of the past 10,000
Friedland offers an arithmetic that makes you squirm: humanity has mined 700 million metric tons of copper in all of history, and to recover all of it you would have to dismantle the US and Europe back to the mammoth age to get back roughly 700 million tons. But at the current pace of the global economy, just sustaining 3% GDP growth — not even counting EVs and data centers — means the next 18 years require mining the same quantity of copper dug up over the past 10,000 years. And people in the industry broadly think that's impossible, because the US has deindustrialized and hasn't built a single copper smelter or nuclear plant since.

22:51 The world's largest copper mine's grade is in free fall
Friedland dissects Escondida: when this, the world's largest copper mine, was discovered a generation ago, its grade was close to 2%; today it has fallen to 0.8%, and within two years it will drop to 0.4%. Falling grade means crushing and grinding more rock to extract less metal, and crushing and grinding accounts for 4% to 5% of global energy consumption. The mine sits at 12,000 feet in the Andes, in the Atacama Desert where it hasn't rained in 30,000 years, and it takes two cubic meters of water to crush one cubic meter of rock. They built a $4 billion desalination plant and spend $1 million a day on electricity pumping water from sea level up to 12,000 feet. The upshot: just keeping this one mine producing requires another $10 to $12 billion of investment.

27:54 An AI search uses 30 times the power of a normal one
Friedland gives a concrete energy comparison: one Google search consumes the electricity to light a 100-watt bulb for 12 seconds, while one AI search — he cites ChatGPT4 and Cloud — uses 30 times that, equivalent to lighting a 100-watt bulb for two or three minutes. Every five-year-old on the planet with an iPad is using AI search, and power demand ‘literally goes to infinity’. He also points out: nothing about the internet is inherently green, and this very studio is itself copper-intensive and energy-intensive.

34:01 Sulfuric acid prices rose more than sixfold in eight months
About 25% of the world's copper needs sulfuric acid for leaching and extraction, and sulfuric acid comes mainly from Middle Eastern natural gas. After the Strait of Hormuz closed, sulfuric acid prices went from $150 a ton to over $1,000 a ton in eight months. Russia and China have already banned sulfuric acid exports. Friedland's company benefits, because it built Africa's largest copper smelter where sulfuric acid is a byproduct — they sell it to fellow copper miners in Congo, at ever higher prices. But he warns: without more sulfuric acid, global food prices will rise too, because sulfuric acid is also used to make fertilizer.

51:25 Buying one large motor means waiting eight years
Friedland tells a supply-chain story absurd in its specificity: building the Oyu Tolgoi copper-gold mine in Mongolia's Gobi Desert required large motors about 40 feet in diameter, and the ring gear alone took four and a half years to arrive. Today the same equipment takes eight to ten years, ‘if ever’. And hyperscalers trying to buy natural gas turbines face lead times of six to eight years. An even more extreme example: a Congo copper mine flooded by an earthquake needed pumps to drain it, pumps moving 1,300 liters per second with a head three times the height of the Eiffel Tower. They called the US and Germany, and neither could build them, because they couldn't get samarium-cobalt magnets. Only China could build them within 30 days. At the time, the flooding was costing $15 million a day in lost revenue.

58:35 US miners earn $100 an hour; Congolese engineers earn $800 a month
Friedland directly compares cost structures: Congo copper grades run 3% to 6%, the median age is 18.7, and a Congolese software engineer who knows AI earns $800 to $1,000 a month. Mining copper in the US, by contrast, means the United Steelworkers demand over $100 an hour for underground work, plus environmental legislation and legal constraints, making costs far higher. He also criticizes the net present value model invented by the financial system: it was designed for oil and gas, but mines can't be shoehorned into it — an oil field decays fast without investment, whereas a mine with 100 years of reserves won't deplete like an oil field. The NPV model suppresses mining company valuations, and today mining companies' total market cap is under 1% of the S&P 500, the lowest ever.

1:02:39 Tariffs could keep US copper mining alive, but they'd stoke inflation
Asked about copper tariffs, Friedland says explicitly he won't take a position, but he can argue both sides: if copper is $6 and you add a 30% tariff, that's $1.8, taking copper to $7.8, and then he can afford to pay American miners, making US mining viable. But the flip side is domestic inflation, possibly higher rates, and with midterms coming, it's a political question. He boils it down to: do you actually want to reindustrialize America? If you can't even build nuclear plants and ships, you lose sovereignty. Last year the US built about 8 ships; China built 1,000.

1:04:42 Governments are quietly stockpiling copper, and nobody can tally supply and demand
Friedland raises an overlooked phenomenon: governments are buying copper as a proxy for money, and not reporting it. He says nobody can calculate the supply-demand balance for any metal, because ‘why would you’. Meanwhile China is buying gold and selling US Treasuries, and a great debasement trade is beginning. Hedge funds borrow yen and depend on yen weakness so they never have to repay. He thinks we're at an inflection point where everything is becoming naked and globally scrutinized.

item.title: Engineers stopped writing code a year ago, AI employees tripled the company
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-twentyvc-工程师一年前就不写代码了-ai-员工让公司规模翻三倍/

item.description: Eight Sleep's email marketing team went from 2 people to 0, with annual revenue approaching $100 million; engineers stopped writing code a year ago, replaced by hundreds of AI engineers. Matteo has started counting "human employees" and "AI employees" — counting AI, the company is three to four times its current size.
item.content:encoded:
Eight Sleep's email marketing team went from 2 people to 0, with annual revenue approaching $100 million; engineers stopped writing code a year ago, replaced by hundreds of AI engineers. Matteo has started counting "human employees" and "AI employees" — counting AI, the company is three to four times its current size.

Medium information density, but there are several concrete numbers and mechanisms worth hearing: how AI employees took over marketing, platform CAC fraud, hardware cost due diligence. The celebrity stories in the second half are soft.

5:10 Salaries are out of control, hiring shifts to Europe
Matteo says we're "back to 2021": not just engineers, even product managers' salaries are out of control, and any company is making crazy offers. The bigger problem isn't hiring but retention — as long as you're a company with a decent brand, employees will keep getting higher-paying offers. Eight Sleep's response is to shift hiring increasingly to Europe and outside the US. He also admits that when the salary gap gets big enough, "there's nothing you can do," and indeed some people have been poached by companies like OpenAI and Anthropic.

7:14 Hardware founders get first-year costs wrong by 50%
Asked what investors don't understand about hardware, Matteo gives a very specific answer: in the first year, even the first three months, founders don't really know what it costs to produce the device, nor what the return rate is. So the BOM and COGS they present when fundraising will be off by at least 50%. This is a due diligence checklist for hardware investors: don't trust the cost structure early founders report.

9:16 Platform-reported CAC is fake, run your own incrementality tests
Matteo says you can't trust platform attribution because the same platform will double-count conversions. For example, Meta's dashboard shows a CAC about 20% lower than the real CAC. Eight Sleep's approach is to build its own model to calculate the true CAC of each channel, and run an incrementality test every six months — for example, turning off a channel in two similar-performing regions and seeing how much revenue drops, thereby calculating the channel's true incremental value. His reasoning is direct: if you don't do this, the brand is only fooling itself.

17:29 Email marketing team went from 2 to 0, annual revenue near $100M
Eight Sleep originally had a two-person email marketing team. After the lead left, co-founder Alexandra took over and within three days built multiple bots to take over all email marketing. Now the team is zero people, and email marketing contributes close to $100 million in revenue. The mechanism: AI decides based on historical data when to send, what email to send, and what copy to use. Matteo also says he has started counting "human employees" and "AI employees," and counting AI employees, the company is about three to four times its current size.

19:39 Engineers stopped writing code a year ago
Matteo says Eight Sleep's engineers stopped writing code about a year ago; now they have hundreds of AI engineers writing for them. This is why the company can expand in 35 countries (including China, the Middle East, Europe — markets with varying regulations) with a very small team. The main tool is Claude, with monthly spending in the millions of dollars. From this he raises an investment question: if 5% of the engineering budget is spent on Claude, will that proportion rise to 50% or be pushed down to 1% by open-source models? His own judgment is that both happen simultaneously — usage rises, unit price falls, net effect is a decline.

26:59 He believes model self-training has already happened
Asked about OpenAI people calling for a "slight pause," Matteo says what's really worrying is the part where models learn on their own and train themselves — that's the starting point of losing control. The host asks, "Don't you think we're already there?" He replies, "I think we're already there," and believes there's a big gap between the capabilities users see and what frontier model companies have internally, the latter having already seen it behind the scenes. He mentions attempts in OpenAI's models where agents form groups on their own.

38:05 Endorsements only with real product users
Matteo says any athlete or celebrity partnership has only two conditions: first, they must actually use the product, preferably having bought it with their own money; second, he must be able to establish a direct relationship with the person, not accept a manager blocking in between. The reason is practical — the greatest value of such a product is that they casually tell friends it's good; if they just got millions of dollars in equity, it's purely a financial transaction and brings nothing.

52:35 Interviewing at both Anthropic and us is a red flag
Matteo says people still tell him, "I'm choosing between Anthropic and Eight Sleep," and he thinks this is a very bad red flag — not because of salary, but because it shows the person hasn't thought it through; the two jobs have nothing in common. When hiring, he cares more about whether the person is driven by the right things, not just comparing prices.

item.title: A US measles death erased from CDC data, and state reporting rights are being taken over by the federal government
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-twiv-美国麻疹死婴被从cdc数据里抹掉-州报告权正在被联邦接管/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-twiv-美国麻疹死婴被从cdc数据里抹掉-州报告权正在被联邦接管/
item.description: The CDC refused to count two Pennsylvania measles deaths in the national tally, citing "insufficient information" — but the CDC itself took part in that investigation. The precedent is more dangerous than the individual case: state reporting has become negotiable.
item.content:encoded:
The CDC refused to count two Pennsylvania measles deaths in the national tally, citing "insufficient information" — but the CDC itself took part in that investigation. The precedent is more dangerous than the individual case: state reporting has become negotiable.

A clinical-update format show: the first stretch is a quick pass over outbreak data, and the two densest segments are the measles death controversy in the middle and the COVID vaccine cardiovascular benefit.

4:06 Florida has local dengue transmission
Griffin says he can now see dengue cases without leaving the country: in the past week alone Florida had 32 locally acquired cases, more than 70 locally acquired dengue cases cumulatively, and 14 virus-positive mosquito pools detected across 5 counties. In the same segment he also mentions a CDC health advisory issued that day — rabies-related consultations since July 2026 are up 17% over the same period in 2025, including mass exposure events, against a backdrop of US pet owners becoming hesitant about vaccinating animals against rabies. Put together, these two things show not an incidental outbreak of some pathogen but that the US has abandoned lines of defense against preventable diseases it mastered decades ago.

6:09 NIH money is being moved to the Department of Defense
Nature reported that NIH is seeking to transfer hundreds of millions of dollars of research projects from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases to the Department of Defense's (referred to in the piece as the Department of War) biodefense programs, and two NIH employees told Nature the two sides had signed a preliminary agreement. The Department of Defense responded confirming it had signed a research agreement allowing "project-by-project strategic collaboration," and said "any suggestion that this agreement was reached in secret is false" — but the response did not mention the money at all. Griffin's follow-up is direct: biodefense itself is fine, the Department of Defense has plenty of money, it does not need to reach into the pockets of an already underfunded NIH.

9:09 HPV vaccination has not risen in four years, only 77.7%
The MMWR adolescent vaccination coverage survey shows HPV vaccine coverage among 13- to 17-year-olds has not risen since 2021, now stalled for a fourth consecutive year: in 2025 only 77.7% had received at least one dose, and only 63.4% completed the series. By comparison, Tdap and meningococcal vaccines have held at about 90% since 2019, with far smaller geographic variation than HPV. The HPV vaccination gap between rural and urban areas exists at every poverty level, whereas the rural-urban gap for meningococcal vaccine appears only among adolescents below the poverty line. Griffin's comment: this vaccine can 100% prevent cervical cancer, anogenital cancers and head and neck cancers, so why isn't it being done.

15:15 Congo Ebola: only 15% of new cases come from known contacts
MMWR used a set of "operational indicators" to assess control of the Democratic Republic of the Congo's 2026 Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak over the 21 days from July 31 to August 21: the average proportion of alerts investigated within 24 hours was 83%, against a target above 90%; only 10.6 contacts on average were identified per confirmed case, against a target above 20; only 15% to 20% of newly confirmed cases had previously been identified as known contacts, against a target above 90%, meaning most cases occur outside known chains of transmission; and 59% of Ebola deaths occurred outside Ebola treatment centers, when that number should be zero. Griffin's conclusion is that the outbreak is far from controlled, with 6,757 confirmed cases and 3,267 deaths cumulatively.

17:16 The CDC removed state-reported measles deaths from the tally
On August 25 the Pennsylvania Department of Health announced two measles-related deaths in Lancaster County, the state's first in 35 years; the next day RFK Jr. suggested on X that the deaths might have been fabricated by the governor's staff. Late on Sunday night, August 30, the CDC published its weekly measles update, replacing the two deaths with an asterisk and saying the available information could not determine whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths. According to The Washington Post and CNN, the decision came from new CDC director Erica Schwarz, at RFK Jr.'s direction. Vincent points out the key: state and local health departments do case investigations, apply the case definition, and report to the CDC; the CDC has no independent investigative authority and historically has only received and aggregated, checking later. This time, though, the CDC was embedded in Pennsylvania's investigation, so the "insufficient information" claim does not hold up.

19:18 Nobody routinely screens the dead for measles
A SIDRAP commentary dismantled the "measles wasn't the direct cause of death" line: clinically there is no admission swab, no routine testing before delivery or surgery, and no laboratory reason to go looking for measles virus in someone without symptoms; CDC guidance to clinicians is to look first at clinical features — fever, cough, rhinitis, conjunctivitis, rash — and only then mention testing. So a positive measles result in a death investigation usually means there was already a clinical or epidemiological reason to test. The piece concedes the probability of an unrelated death coinciding with an unrelated measles infection is not zero, but small enough that a rational person should shift their judgment substantially. In the Pennsylvania case specifically: the mother also became severely ill after another child was infected with measles, delivered about a month early, and the infant was born not breathing and could not be resuscitated, with measles virus detected in lung tissue.

22:20 The structure of the death certificate is being used as a shield
Much of the controversy stems from how death certificates are structured, something most people have never had reason to learn. Part one lists the causal chain leading to death, with the top line the immediate cause, the lines below it the conditions that produced it, and the last line the underlying cause that started the whole sequence; part two, per the National Center for Health Statistics handbook, is "other significant conditions contributing to death." So the immediate cause line reads pneumonia, encephalitis, or in this case splenic rupture, while measles appears in part two — measles caused the splenic rupture, and the splenic rupture killed the child. Treating "the immediate cause wasn't measles" as evidence measles was irrelevant mistakes the structure of a form for a medical conclusion.

24:20 The real damage is the precedent, not these two cases
Vincent lays out the consequence clearly: if the CDC can refuse to accept a state's statutory report until it is satisfied, then the national count becomes negotiable, and every state's data is subject to federal review under undisclosed standards. Former CDC medical examiner Deb Hury said in a STAT interview that states have always reported deaths and the CDC has always counted them. Pennsylvania also pushed back on the federal account of "what information was actually provided," saying both deaths were reported to the CDC's measles response team, that the state epidemiologist conducted a thorough investigation, and that, per the Pennsylvania health commissioner, the CDC was in fact embedded in that investigation. Griffin adds: whichever team is in power now, someday the other team will be, and the federal government should not be touching the data.

item.title: The AI Doom Narrative Is a Psyop, and the Target Is Open Source
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-allin-ai-末日论是场心理战-靶子是开源/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-allin-ai-末日论是场心理战-靶子是开源/
item.description: Anthropic asks public markets to underwrite it at a trillion-dollar valuation while its safety lead endorses the claim that AI may end civilization — not an internal contradiction, but regulatory groundwork aimed ultimately at open source.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic asks public markets to underwrite it at a trillion-dollar valuation while its safety lead endorses the claim that AI may end civilization — not an internal contradiction, but regulatory groundwork aimed ultimately at open source.

The first half is the sparring over Doomer PR and IPO disclosure; the second half's breakdown of OpenAI's math breakthrough and Nike's collapse is worth more.

0:00 The resignation letter wasn't spontaneous — it was organized PR
Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic after only six weeks and posted that the people building AI genuinely believe it could kill everyone by the end of this decade. Sachs points out this was not spontaneous: the account had almost zero followers and zero posts before, yet got hundreds of millions of views in a day; within the first 15 minutes three Doomer organizations amplified it, all funded by the same big EA donor, who also co-led Anthropic's Series A. More tellingly, the Wall Street Journal story went out minutes before the tweetstorm — meaning the reporter had been briefed under embargo. Sachs says if Coxon really came on the show, the first question would be: who introduced you to the Wall Street Journal?

6:12 The company didn't distance itself — it amplified him
A normal company facing a whistleblower immediately pushes back and distances itself. Anthropic did the opposite: Evan Hubinger, who runs alignment, publicly replied that Jacob is right, that they genuinely believe AI could kill all of humanity, and that he personally puts the probability above 10% over the next decade. Sachs argues this exposes the contradiction — what he said matches the company's internal Doomer agenda exactly, which is why he got internal support. Chamath adds the knife: the company can't distance itself, because the moment it does, that whole internal bloc blows up.

10:18 Asking for a trillion-dollar valuation while saying the product could end civilization
Sachs lays out Anthropic's IPO dilemma clearly: you are asking public-market investors to underwrite your company at a trillion-dollar valuation while your safety lead says the core product is unsolved and could end civilization. That is at minimum the seedbed of product-liability litigation. Chamath uses the Philip Morris analogy: we know cigarettes kill you, we'll say so, but we won't disclose it, we'll still go public and let you buy the stock, and we'll figure it out later. Sachs calls it "a time for choosing" — either publicly deny that Coxon is a Doomer operation, or admit Bernie Sanders is right and development should be frozen, in which case how do you IPO at a trillion-dollar valuation?

22:45 The real target of regulation is open source
Sachs is blunt: this is a Doomer psyop, and the end goal is open source. Because FDA-style regulation won't say "ban open source" — it will say "the same standards apply to open and closed models" — and Dario has already testified in the Senate that models are dangerous if they can't be centrally monitored and rolled back. Once open-model weights are released they can't be rolled back, so the standard landing is equivalent to banning the release, use and hosting of those weights. Freeberg adds: open source has no corporate structure to file regulatory paperwork, and open source is precisely what cut AI costs by 50x and benefited everyone. Chamath's version: once open source is banned, you get a monopoly in partnership with the federal government.

39:17 AI can't even nail autocomplete yet
The core anti-Doomer argument isn't theoretical speculation but everyday experience: autocomplete still isn't good, and AI can't even handle a chore like "bring the toiletry bag upstairs." If it can't finish one mundane task, why believe it can kill all of humanity? They call this humanity's insurance against AI taking over the world — company decisions still require humans to wake up, drink coffee and sit in the same room, and there is a natural 16-hour window between decisions.

50:45 What's truly damning is that retweet endorsement
From a legal standpoint, the key isn't Jacob Coxon's resignation tweet but Evan Hubinger's endorsement retweet — he is still a senior alignment executive at the company, running one of the safety teams, and his co-sign plus the "greater than 10% probability" figure is what made it go viral. If it were only Coxon, the company could call him a disgruntled employee; but an executive endorsement turns "was disclosure adequate" into a real question.

1:00:12 OpenAI solved the math problem with brute force, not divine inspiration
The Navier-Stokes solution used roughly 130 billion output tokens, with 10,000 agents communicating with each other, equivalent to between 50,000 and 500,000 years of human work (estimated at 40 words per minute of typing). AI had no flash of insight humans couldn't have; it just did a huge amount of brute-force work, and every step of the message chain is recorded and human-readable. The conclusion is that AI is a leverage tool, not a math god above humans.

1:15:40 De-identification doesn't remove the method itself
De-identification can strip personal information and company-specific information, but the general method for solving a math problem is itself IP. A user iterates on that method inside the tool, and that conversation can be de-identified and used for training, making the model better at math. This is the network effect of closed models: they can see what the whole world is doing, and this observation system feeds them more data than anyone else, constituting a long-term advantage over customers.
