item.description: Alliance Bernstein relocated from New York to Nashville, saving roughly $85 million a year, and it did not force a single portfolio manager to move — the savings come from real estate and people costs, and the bet is on hiring people New York cannot.
item.content:encoded:
Alliance Bernstein relocated from New York to Nashville, saving roughly $85 million a year, and it did not force a single portfolio manager to move — the savings come from real estate and people costs, and the bet is on hiring people New York cannot.

A 32-year JPMorgan veteran explains the structural shifts in asset management: active to passive, ETFs replacing mutual funds, private credit entering 401ks. Medium information density; the second half is worth more than the first.

9:18 When passive squeezes active, cut costs before talking growth
The Alliance Bernstein Bernstein took over was hitting the biggest industry headwind since the financial crisis: money moving from active to passive, fees compressing across the board, institutional sales commissions falling from 20 to 25 cents a share all the way to a few cents or less than a cent. The firm itself had just been through a collapse — post-merger AUM had touched nearly $900 billion mid-quarter, and by 2012 only $380 billion remained; in 2006 roughly 70% was equity assets, and by 2012 only 30%. His predecessor, brought in from Goldman Sachs, restructured, replaced part of the teams, and equity performance began to recover, which is what got the firm back to net inflows. Bernstein says what he brought was not firefighting but a more global perspective and an emphasis on distribution.

21:39 Moving to Nashville saves $85 million a year, with no forced relocations
The firm was debating whether it could still afford a New York headquarters, and ultimately chose Nashville from five candidate cities — the reason being that it wanted to be a big fish in a small pond, which it could not do in Charlotte or Dallas. The move saves roughly $85 million a year, part real estate and part people. The key design: no portfolio manager was forced to move, because the firm is a price-taker for that kind of talent. As a result, close to 100 portfolio managers moved voluntarily. The challenges are concrete too: Nashville is the capital of healthcare services, and locally it is hard to find international tax accountants and technology and operations people with traditional Wall Street training; but the firm received a flood of résumés from Atlanta, Chicago, New York, Boston and the West Coast.

25:44 Sell-side research without cross-subsidy can only be a joint venture
Bernstein says a buy-side firm owning a sell-side research business is a historical accident. Almost every peer uses equity capital markets or prime brokerage to cross-subsidize its research department, and Alliance Bernstein had no such businesses to subsidize with. So they put the research business into a joint venture with Société Générale, and made clear it would eventually transition entirely to SocGen. He specifically notes the other side's concern was culture — a large French institution facing a group of Americans and Brits — so it had to be done step by step, very carefully. The transition period runs five years from the JV's anniversary, and they are still midway through it.

37:08 Banks are structurally unsuited to holding long-dated fixed-rate assets
Bernstein uses his experience running leveraged finance at JPMorgan to explain the structural opportunity in private credit: banks are highly leveraged players funded short, structurally unsuited to holding long-duration assets, especially fixed-rate ones. JPMorgan at the time spent a great deal of time and money trying to securitize its loan book, and credit derivatives started there. Insurance companies and funds are a better home for these assets, because funds do not offer a genuine liquidity option and therefore have no run risk. He states plainly that there is no maturity transformation in credit, and apart from interest and principal there should never be any liquidity at all.

40:14 Private credit's problem is not defaults, it is insufficient disclosure
Asked how the industry gets past the first half of this year, Bernstein's answer is education and transparency: tell clients how many names are on the watch list, how many have stopped accruing interest. He says there is currently no mandatory disclosure obligation, but regular updates to clients make them more comfortable, and one should over-communicate in periods like this. He also frames the problem as structural rather than systemic: defaults are simply the normal course of lending, and models typically already build in 2%, 3%, 4% default expectations; what went wrong was a handful of companies, plus fraud, which has always existed; what genuinely went wrong was that structure and pricing got out of balance for a time. His conclusion is that after going through this, now is actually a better entry point.

43:14 Private credit in 401ks: fees are not the obstacle
Bernstein thinks target-date funds and 401ks may be exactly the right place for private credit: demand is highly predictable, professional managers make the decisions, and plan sponsors are themselves sophisticated investors. Alliance Bernstein worked with Brookfield and Carlyle to develop vehicles that can sit alongside target-date funds, building diversified exposure to private credit, private equity and private real estate. He concedes the industry has been too optimistic about the pace of adoption, that plan sponsors are conservative, and that this will take many years, but in ten years it will most likely be part of large plans. On the objection about fees, his response: these are institutional buyers and they will bargain hard; and private assets are only a small slice of a target-date portfolio, so the impact on total fees is limited.

47:18 Retirement planning should go through retirement, not stop at it
Bernstein points to Australia's superannuation funds as an example, saying they are thought leaders on how to think about retirement, and that one key practice is designing the glide path to go through retirement rather than stop at it. His reasoning: what most people need least at 65 is to hold mostly short-term fixed income and cash, because they may have another 20 to 25 years to live. More practically, many people have not saved enough to retire, and will delay retirement and look for supplemental income. He also proposes a specific mechanism: rather than buying an annuity in one lump at retirement, design the target-date fund to leave a pool of liquidity at age 75 to buy an annuity, which can significantly lower the cost of the annuity while extending income protection over a longer lifespan.

51:26 AB is the last publicly traded partnership
Bernstein says AB is probably the last publicly traded partnership, a structure rare outside energy MLPs. It means issuing K-1 tax forms, and institutions have an allergic reaction to K-1s, which limits their willingness to hold the stock. He describes the stock as a bond with an equity option attached — essentially high-yield debt plus an equity kicker. Asked why not change the structure and make the stock pop, his answer is direct: if they changed the structure and the stock did not pop, a lot of people would be unhappy; and most shareholders would be negatively affected on taxes, so the board has to consider it, but the honest answer is that it is not a sure thing.

item.title: AI 2040 Isn't About Stopping AI, It's About Delaying Superintelligence to 2040
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-tbpn-ai-2040-不是停掉-ai-是把超级智能推迟到-2040/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-tbpn-ai-2040-不是停掉-ai-是把超级智能推迟到-2040/
item.description: The real mechanism behind the anti-AI proposal is a compute cap: pause new frontier training, allow inference only, and make weight theft impossible with a 1 MB/s external link and a Faraday cage.
item.content:encoded:
The real mechanism behind the anti-AI proposal is a compute cap: pause new frontier training, allow inference only, and make weight theft impossible with a 1 MB/s external link and a Faraday cage.

High information density, but the topics jump around: AI regulation, robotics, how VCs read people, and the chip supply chain each get a segment — good for listening selectively.

0:00 AI 2040 doesn't stop AI, it delays it to 2040
Many people assume anti-AI sentiment is pushing to ‘stop AI’, but what the AI 2040 proposal actually says is: keep inference on existing models, keep doing capability research, and just push superintelligence from 2028 to 2040. The concrete mechanism is a compute cap — pause new frontier training, apply ‘inference-only verification’ to data centers above 10,000 H100-equivalents (roughly $100M of equipment), and physically rip out the high-bandwidth east-west networking inside the data center so distributed training can't run but inference proceeds as normal. New R&D centers would have to be built from scratch inside a Faraday cage, with external connectivity capped at 1 MB/s — stealing the weights would take five years.

0:00 Anti-AI mobilization is nowhere near anti-battery-chicken
Speaker 2 points out a contrast: the anti-flock (anti-battery-chicken) movement converts into real physical action by ordinary people, whereas on the anti-AI side you don't see a 100,000-like video teaching people ‘how to cut power to your local data center’. Speaker 1 adds that anti-AI volume comes more from concrete self-interest of the ‘I'm an artist and I don't like AI-generated images’ kind than from x-risk arguments. Data centers sit in remote locations, behind fences, heavily fortified — far harder to get at than a chicken coop on the street.

0:00 The compute cap is the valve easiest to turn
The most effective control lever in the proposal is judged to be the compute cap: chip controls plus slower data center construction. The goal is to make models stronger mainly by adding hardware rather than by new algorithms — because algorithmic breakthroughs can be hidden inside secret projects. Speaker 1 notes that Ilya's new lab recently got a large cluster from NVIDIA; even people on an orthogonal research path have to stack compute, which suggests ‘scale is a prerequisite’ is basically consensus in this circle.

0:00 Doomists don't bet, because they wouldn't live to collect
Tyler Cowen demands that pessimists name the corresponding market price to validate their belief, but Deep Dish counters: why should a short-term existential risk be reflected in market prices? ‘If everyone's dead, the contract that pays out is worthless to me.’ Speaker 5 twists the knife: in the nuclear war era people built bunkers; nobody builds an AI bunker, because everyone thinks it's too totalizing for a bunker to help — so ‘you didn't build a bunker’ doesn't prove you don't believe. Paul Christiano was dug up as being 2x levered long and short 30-year US Treasuries, but that bet also pays off in the ‘good ending’, unlike a doomsday wager.

0:00 The fruit fly agent moves the moral question forward
Google mapped every neuron of the fruit fly, and once the code was open-sourced people started messing with it in every way: someone put the fruit fly agent inside a Rabbit R1, and shaking the device makes its escape circuit light up; someone else made it play Doom. Speaker 1 thinks the real question is the next stop on this road — if you can simulate a human, converse with it, and it behaves like a human, does it have moral status? His own judgment is not to overthink it, and not to be in the business of torturing anything. He also mentions that last night he had Astra play Balatro using computer use, and it felt like giving it a reward rather than torturing it.

0:00 Once a reporter is in the room, he stops being escorted out
Alex Heath describes the core mechanism of his changed status: when a reporter is in the room, you're brought in and then immediately escorted out; now he gets to stay in the room and slowly marinate on it. So his newsletter perspective changes — instead of landing a scoop, he distills a large volume of off-the-record conversation into a judgment, such as the personal agents piece he's writing. He states clearly that confidentiality still matters, and he won't leak memos companies are worried about again — ten years of that is enough.

0:00 A newcomer can't easily replicate his path now
Asked whether now is a good time to become the next Alex Heath, his answer is the opposite: the traditional media environment is structurally challenged, many places aren't hiring, traffic is declining, and they haven't pivoted to direct models like subscriptions and streaming. The only viable path he offers is ‘maniacally focus on one thing and become the best in the world at that’ — he himself started by focusing on covering Snap, broke a pile of Snap news, and after being noticed migrated that capability to other companies. And the niche has to be the intersection of niche and matters, not just obscure.

0:00 Fear of being left behind hands new players an opening
A host other than Mitesh proposes a counterintuitive mechanism: because people fear AI, they're more willing to try new products — they don't want to be left behind, don't want to become a permanent underclass. The result is that people who have used various AI products for years are still willing to try new things, which keeps creating second- and third-mover advantage. At the same time, once an AI brand gets big it starts accumulating baggage, and people become more willing to share and discuss something new rather than the one they use every day. That leaves a lot of room for startups.

item.title: The Oldest Manuscript of The Song of Roland Is Actually an English Performance Copy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-britishhist-最古老的-罗兰之歌-抄本-其实是个英国人的演出本/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-britishhist-最古老的-罗兰之歌-抄本-其实是个英国人的演出本/
item.description: The Oxford Digby 23 manuscript is written in Anglo-Norman, and scholars date it to between 1140 and 1170 by tracking dialect drift — the most complete version of this French epic was performed for the English.
item.content:encoded:
The Oxford Digby 23 manuscript is written in Anglo-Norman, and scholars date it to between 1140 and 1170 by tracking dialect drift — the most complete version of this French epic was performed for the English.

This is a members-only sample episode, medium information density, but it gets very concrete about how a manuscript gets read as "some minstrel's working copy" — good for listeners interested in manuscripts, oral epic and dialect reconstruction.

1:03 The most complete version is an English manuscript
The Song of Roland is a French epic that took shape around the 12th century, belonging to the genre Chanson de Geste (songs of deeds), and it spread with 12th-century French cultural hegemony to regions including Britain. But its most complete and oldest surviving version is not from France itself — it is an English manuscript, catalogued as Oxford Digby 23. This manuscript was originally bound together with a completely unrelated book by someone later, which is why it is called Digby 23 B, and A is that "other book." Nobody knows who bound them together; possibly some monk felt both were his favourite books.

3:05 Every stanza is a camera position
The poem is organised in laisses (stanzas) of varying length, and each laisse is like a camera focus: when the scene or the mood shifts, you change laisse. The whole poem is in decasyllabic meter, cut into four plus six in performance: the first four syllables rise, then a dramatic pause, then the last six syllables fall, overall close to iambic turning into trochaic. Recited over and over this becomes hypnotic, and the poem runs to four thousand lines — hours of recitation.

7:27 At peak emotion, the same action is performed three times
This kind of epic has a convention that is hard for any reteller to handle: when the action is especially intense or the emotion especially strong, it uses consecutive laisses to tell the same action from three angles, a kind of poetic slow motion. For example, Roland's refusal to blow the oliphant is told three times, with almost no gap between them. This is also why it reads like an action film or a comic: scenes cut hard, with no softening transition — for instance, "Roland dies, his soul ascends to heaven" is followed directly by "the Emperor arrives at Roncevaux."

9:29 The performer's name is left at the end of the manuscript
Digby 23 is very likely a real minstrel's working copy. Line 4002 of the poem, its final line, says roughly: "here ends the song of deeds; Turoldus will not tell more." This line appears before Charlemagne's lament, so it reads more like the performer saying: this is too sad, I cannot go on. The name Turoldus does not appear in the poem, and he is not a known scribe, so scholars lean towards him being the owner of this manuscript, the performer of this performance.

10:31 Its pocket-book size gives away that it was for work
The manuscript is only about six and a half inches by four and a half inches, a pocket book you could carry on your person, not a wealthy man's finely bound volume. It is itself heavily worn and not refined, and it contains some small annotations of unclear meaning. Together these features point to a professional performer on the move: he might have travelled alone with an instrument, or been the lead singer or narrator in a troupe, with someone in front of him doing the physical performance. Such people were jongleurs — the origin of the later word juggler.

12:31 The dialect pins this performer to England
The manuscript is not in the French of central France, nor continental French, but in Anglo-Norman, which suggests this performer was probably Anglo-Norman, performing in Britain or at least in Normandy. The dialect features are very specific: continental French O and OU are replaced by U, so Roland becomes Rulant, l'or becomes l'ur; Anglo-Norman French was also losing final soft e. These changes even begin to break the originally strict decasyllabic meter, leaving some lines with only nine syllables or swelling to eleven.

14:34 Accent drift alone can date a manuscript
Scholars' grasp of this dialect is fine enough that they can date the manuscript to between 1140 and 1170 based on the degree of accent drift. The method is similar to scholars reconstructing Shakespearean pronunciation, tracking regular changes in syllables and sounds. Poetry is especially suited to this kind of reconstruction, because meter and rhyme expose which sounds were dropped and which were added. For many jongleurs, French was a second language anyway, spoken with a dialect accent, and they spelled by sound.

17:40 A French epic, an English artefact
Although this is a French poem about an old French king, this manuscript is an English thing, performed for Britons at the time. There is no equally complete other manuscript to compare line by line, but there are abundant records of The Song of Roland being sung before and after this manuscript, and scholars can use them to judge where this performer departed from what the genre should look like. The episode goes on to cover the poem's symbolic system, how its audience was constructed, and what the music sounded like.

item.title: The Army Secretary Resigns: The People Who Can Actually Fight Get Cleared Out First
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-chinatalk-陆军部长辞职-最会打仗的人先被清掉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-chinatalk-陆军部长辞职-最会打仗的人先被清掉/
item.description: Twenty-five years after 9/11, the US military never got off the treadmill: budgets eaten by war, transformation forced through on cheap technology, and the officers who understand tech and are willing to take risks are being cleared out batch by batch.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, the US military never got off the treadmill: budgets eaten by war, transformation forced through on cheap technology, and the officers who understand tech and are willing to take risks are being cleared out batch by batch.

The first half — 9/11 reflection and Army personnel insider detail — is dense; the second half, on AI battlefields and model distillation, is more casual chat, so the first half alone is worth it.

3:03 The war on terror ate the money for military transformation
Before 9/11 the US military was transforming as Rumsfeld demanded, under the expectation of a relatively comfortable budget environment in which new technology could be slipped into the force gradually. Then GWAT arrived, all available resources were sucked into the war, and the transformation directive remained while the money was gone. Hence a run of procurement disasters: the Army's Future Combat Systems, the Navy's Ford-class carrier, the Littoral Combat Ship, DDG-1000 Zumwalt, and the CGX that was simply never built. Brian's judgment is that the technology jumped too far, the investment was nowhere near enough, and everyone was distracted supporting a war that had just started, so these programs were doomed. The troubles with today's B-21 and F-35 trace back to this period too.

5:22 Twenty-five years on a treadmill, never actually stopping
Tony points out that op-tempo never stopped after it started in 2001: 12-month, 15-month deployment rotations, and the National Guard is still deploying at home and abroad today. Killing Bin Laden in 2011 could have been a high point, but nothing changed afterward — deployments continued, and through the fall of Kabul, they were still deploying. No one has fully calculated what 25 straight years in that state costs an army. Brian adds a mechanism: conventional forces used to train at home, reset, and move through a training progression, and that rhythm disappeared, replaced by "preparing for the next deployment," so there is no time to test new technology or study new ways of fighting.

7:31 MRAP thinking: use a bigger truck to stop anti-tank missiles
Brian gives an example absurd in its specificity. In Syria the threat was not IEDs but ATGMs (anti-tank guided weapons, similar to Russian TOW variants). The commander's reflex was to stuff everyone into MRAPs — making the vehicles bigger, which made them easier for ATGMs to spot, while MRAP armor cannot stop munitions designed to penetrate tanks. His conclusion: risk calculation in the war-on-terror era has gone so deep that commanders cannot reconceptualize even a small tactical adjustment. This is also the direct consequence of why so many commanders today struggle to adapt to Ukraine and the Lisko battlefield, and cannot imagine how tactics will change.

9:37 Get used to zero casualties and you can't accept dying
Brian says that after 9/11 the US military became increasingly risk- and casualty-averse. The Littoral Combat Ship debate is the specimen: opponents said the ship couldn't take a hit and would be sunk the moment war started; the original proposers answered that it was never going to be sent into a major war, and if it got ambushed and sunk, that was the risk you take for serving. That logic was completely unacceptable on Capitol Hill — Iraq and Afghanistan pushed casualties far below the levels of past wars, everyone got used to it, and so they cannot accept that against a peer opponent a great many people will probably die. The result is continuing to build "Death Star"-style big ships and big platforms, hoping they can protect themselves, rather than going with smaller, more distributed approaches that accept a different risk structure.

10:39 Twenty-five years surrounding Iran, but no network built
Brian says this is the most important lesson he took from 9/11, and it came from a friend's reminder: over 25 years the US basically surrounded Iran, and the CIA's and part of special operations' job was to develop networks and identify people who could oppose an oppressive regime, in case a moment of change came. But when the shooting against Iran started six months ago, it looked like very little network- and capacity-building had been done in those 25 years. The reason is a mental shift: GWAT focused on counterinsurgency and catching bad guys, not the long-term unconventional warfare of pre-positioning for a future conflict — how to support an insurgency inside a regime you might someday want to overthrow. In his words, everyone was too busy stabilizing the situation rather than destabilizing.

13:53 Driscoll resigns, and from here on it's all acting officials
Tony recaps: George was fired, Driscoll went to the White House, said "everything is terrible," and resigned that week. The backdrop is the Army being meddled with back and forth by OSD and the Secretary of the Army's office, plus personality clashes. What he hears is that Congress will not confirm anyone else Pete nominates, so either they bring in someone both the White House and Congress can accept but Pete doesn't like, or they just keep using acting officials. He judges this is the start of the rest of this administration being "stuck with acting officials": after the midterms the House flips at least, the Senate either flips or goes 50:50, no one has the energy to push this kind of person through, and so acting officials, continued OSD meddling, and low morale will persist.

14:54 The drone battalion is disbanded, and the ability to experiment goes with it
The Army decided around the same time to dissolve its newly created drone battalion — a battalion meant to absorb Ukraine's experience directly and then study how to embed it in infantry battalions. Tony concedes there is a good argument that "it shouldn't exist in just one battalion": concentrating lessons in a central warehouse strips every commander of the responsibility to think about their own organization. But his worry is that the Army still needs a unit that can run experiments, run tests, and allow failure; cutting it in the name of "uniformity" loses the ability to experiment, and the force will stand still. He also names Chris Donahue as sacrificed: a commander widely recognized as understanding technology, its effects, and how to run international partnerships, done in over the Abbey Gate bombing (not his fault) and a photo a reporter took.

21:03 Confidence is lost in layers, by rank
Tony breaks morale down by rank: junior officers are still early but already thinking "garrison isn't what I signed up for," and that if you're not garrisoning you're going out to get hit by missiles; field-grade officers are starting to agonize over whether they have to make political decisions just to stay; senior field-grade officers and junior generals are basically "all in or burned out." He says the whole force is tired, and this doesn't look like the Army they joined. And in interviewees' telling, the Iran war is more of a tipping point than Donahue's departure — many O-4s and O-5s he knows originally supported this administration and are furious after the Donahue affair. Brian adds: people like Donahue are the true product of elite selection, and cutting them makes you doubt the claim that promotion is "by ability alone."

item.title: AI researchers sped up 10x in two years, but RSI may be easier than being a paralegal

item.description: RSI is a cumulative task: in theory a Python file under a million tokens could train a recursively self-improving model from scratch. A law firm's paralegal, by contrast, has to remember shifting interpersonal relationships and tacit ways of doing things — a non-stationary distribution.
item.content:encoded:
RSI is a cumulative task: in theory a Python file under a million tokens could train a recursively self-improving model from scratch. A law firm's paralegal, by contrast, has to remember shifting interpersonal relationships and tacit ways of doing things — a non-stationary distribution.

The three researchers' disagreements about RSI, continual learning and RL generalisation are very concrete, and the second half's mechanistic explanation of mid-training and signal-to-noise is the most valuable part of the episode.

0:00 A model looks smart, then a month later looks dumb again
John Schulman describes a recurring loop: a new model comes out, people are blown away and say "this is AGI", but after about a month of use it starts to look dumb again. The loop may keep repeating, and it's hard to predict how many more times. His mechanism: capability doesn't explode right now because you still get bottlenecked doing research and engineering — even if a model can write far more code than a person, it doesn't give you a 100x productivity gain. Dwarkesh opens by asking: if there's no crazy alien superintelligence by 2036, what's the most likely technical reason? Beren Millidge's default answer is a Moravec-paradox-style continuation — AI does superbly at whatever humans put into a benchmark or environment, but a stubborn sim-to-real gap always stands in the way.

18:39 Distillation is the only force against centralisation
John Schulman sees distillation as the main force countering the centralisation trend: anything learnable through RL can be distilled easily, because the number of bits is small and a little data suffices. But he stresses distillation isn't trivial — when you distill with supervised learning the prompt distribution matters enormously, and you need a real, broad prompt distribution. He mentions something that has recently surfaced: some Chinese companies may be running router services that let Chinese users access otherwise-blocked US frontier models, and these services collect and sell data, which is an extremely useful dataset for distillation because it gives you a perfect prompt distribution. Charlie O'Neill draws a concrete prediction from this: frontier labs may not have much of an edge on RL environments after all.

44:38 RSI is a cumulative task; being a lawyer is not
Charlie O'Neill splits tasks into two kinds: cumulative and non-stationary. RSI is cumulative — in theory a Python file under a million tokens could train a recursively self-improving model from scratch, and once you discover attention, mixture of experts or GRPO you just add it to the training stack without going back to the start. The real world is not cumulative: a law firm's paralegal has to remember the shifting relationships among everyone important at the company and all the tacit ways of doing things, which is a non-stationary distribution. Dwarkesh's summary: "RSI just happens to be easier than being a paralegal, which is very unfortunate." If labs conclude RSI is cumulative, more compute will tilt that way.

52:00 Continual learning is stuck on catastrophic forgetting
Charlie O'Neill says the outer loop of pouring data into mid-training at large scale and large batch does work, but at the micro level — a model doing several hundred consecutive small updates for one law firm — every method breaks down: SFT on successful trajectories causes catastrophic forgetting and general capability degrades; on-policy distillation pushes that boundary a bit further out but eventually yields too. RL is good at instilling capabilities and bad at instilling knowledge. Beren Millidge thinks this is mainly a technical problem, not a capacity problem: a model of the same size pretrained from scratch on all the data is simply better, and the bottleneck is plasticity and catastrophic forgetting, with no good way to stop old data being forgotten.

59:46 Data explains 12x; architecture explains only 3.7x
Dwarkesh and Princeton's Jerry Han ran a grid experiment: pairing training recipes and datasets from 2019 to now in every combination, GPT-2 with the latest Ultra-FineWeb, Delphi with an old dataset like Pile, running the whole grid. The conclusion is that data gives roughly a 12.0x compute-efficiency gain, while architecture improvements give only about 3.7x, and at very small scale. Charlie O'Neill says the big chunk that is the internet has already been eaten, useful things won't keep growing at the same rate, and there's probably only a pile of 0.1% loss reductions left. He notes someone at Epoch estimated 3x per year since 2019, over 2000x cumulative, and the missing 100x probably comes from post-training.

1:03:00 RL needs a curriculum; pretraining doesn't
Beren Millidge says this comes back to the RL signal problem: RL is currently bad at exploration, and if the model can't get it in 128 rollouts there's basically no learning signal, so RL needs curricula while pretraining needs none at all. Charlie O'Neill adds: the pretraining signal is already in Common Crawl, the problem is just filtering out noise, which can be automated; but once you get to mid-training and post-training the signal simply isn't in the raw data, and no amount of filtering will pull it out — there isn't a Millennium Prize proof hiding in Common Crawl waiting to be filtered out. You have to get the bits from elsewhere: have people write out reasoning traces, construct environments, or use human data from deployment.

1:18:03 Most of RL's success comes from mid-training
Beren Millidge says what's underrated is mid-training: pretraining on synthetic reasoning data and environments, warm-starting the model to where it has almost completed 80% of the path to the final RL checkpoint, with RL only fine-tuning the policy on top. So it doesn't need to learn these behaviours from scratch, and a few bits per episode suffice. He also stresses that the signal-to-noise ratio of those bits is far higher than ordinary pretraining — in SFT you have to match another model's reasoning process token by token, which pours in too many bits about "how it thinks" and drowns the signal; RL's objective ignores all the other bits and keeps only "did it get the answer right".

1:28:32 One year or three, the difference is long-tail chores
Asked when you could hire a drop-in remote white-collar worker, Charlie O'Neill says if it has to operate a browser, probably a few years; if it can be given Slack and programmatic access, probably a year. Beren Millidge says full generality might take three years, but organisations will actively reshape themselves to be more AI-friendly, so you get 80-90% before then. The substance of the disagreement is the long tail: some chores humans can do will take the model a very long time. Charlie gives the example that the model won't "yell at people" to push work forward — it's too nice. John Schulman points out that human remote workers already vary enormously in quality, and on Upwork it's often hard to get someone doing a software project to take feedback seriously; in some cases the pre-AI version is worse than today's AI.

item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-moneystuff-快船用假代言绕工资帽-nba-请律所查出了更多/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-moneystuff-快船用假代言绕工资帽-nba-请律所查出了更多/
item.description: Wachtell's independent investigation did not clear the Clippers — it made the scandal bigger: beyond Aspiration, there is a string of fake endorsements funded by the Clippers that ended up flowing to Kawhi Leonard.
item.content:encoded:
Wachtell's independent investigation did not clear the Clippers — it made the scandal bigger: beyond Aspiration, there is a string of fake endorsements funded by the Clippers that ended up flowing to Kawhi Leonard.

The first half is dense with sports-scandal detail; the real value is in the second half — Apollo's "jerk premium" and the Cede & Co stock custody mechanism.

2:04 The Clippers used fake endorsements to get around the salary cap
The Clippers first paid millions of dollars to a company called Aspiration Partners, nominally for vague environmental services; Aspiration then paid that money to Kawhi Leonard in the form of endorsement fees, while Leonard did almost no endorsing. When Pablo Torre first reported it, the claim was still disputed, and the Clippers consistently denied it, but the investigation the NBA commissioned from Wachtell Lipton basically confirmed it — and found more similar arrangements.

4:09 Even the scoreboard company was pulled in to move the money
The Wachtell report found more than just the Aspiration payment. The Clippers also paid "consulting fees" to companies that provided no consulting services at all, including the company that made the scoreboard for their arena. The method: the Clippers would pay a consulting fee, then call and ask for a higher purchase price on the scoreboard, with the clear expectation that the other side would pass the money on to Kawhi Leonard. The money went in a circle, and the ultimate purpose was still to give the star player a raise.

7:09 An independent law firm investigation is not there to clear you
Max had assumed an outside law firm's independent investigation was meant to produce a clean bill of health after a scandal, but the Wachtell report made things look worse. Matt offers a more cynical explanation: the classic use of a law firm investigation, under the shadow of a DOJ or regulatory probe, is to hand over some "bad apple" as a scapegoat so the company gets credit for cooperating. But this time there was no DOJ pressure to shut down the NBA, the NBA seems to have given Wachtell a lot of room, and Wachtell clearly had a great time digging.

10:14 Once the DAT premium vanished, the arbitrage ran in reverse
Empery Digital was originally an electric motorcycle company, and in July 2025 it transformed into a digital asset treasury company (DAT), stockpiling about $500 million of bitcoin, with its stock at one point trading at a premium to its holdings. The logic: put $1 of bitcoin into a DAT and it becomes $2 of stock. But the premium quickly disappeared and DATs began trading at a discount, so the arbitrage flipped — use $0.90 of stock to buy $1 of bitcoin, buy the DAT, break it up, sell the bitcoin. DAT activism was born.

17:20 Is a shareholder shorting bitcoin disloyal?
One of the core disputes in the Empery case: an activist buys discounted DAT stock while shorting an equal amount of bitcoin, achieving delta neutrality and earning only the discount convergence. The company argues this must be disclosed, because the other shareholders are all theoretically long bitcoin, while these people are bitcoin-neutral, their interests are not aligned, and they should not be eligible to run for the board. Matt thinks the argument is "wrong, but only accidentally wrong": if the DAT is a vehicle for believers to hold bitcoin (like Strategy), it makes sense; but most DAT shareholders are the same hedge funds, all of whom came for the premium and are unhappy about the discount, so their interests are actually aligned.

23:26 Cede & Co holds most American stocks
Matt mentions a fact in his column that most people don't know: most shares of most American companies are registered in the name of Cede & Co, the nominee of DTC. A 1998 report said Cede & Co held 83% of all US stocks; DTC now custodies about $74 trillion of stock. When you hold shares through Robinhood, what actually happens is that Robinhood has a record on DTC's ledger, and Cede & Co is on the company's shareholder register. The system grew out of the efficiency revolution of the 1960s and 70s, when paper stock certificates were centralised in one place and only name changes were recorded.

27:31 Robinhood's tokenisation is not an on-chain shareholder register
Tokenised stocks can mean many things, and one ideal is this: every company maintains a public blockchain shareholder register, no longer needing intermediaries like DTC or Robinhood, and the company can build a direct relationship with its shareholders. But that is not what Robinhood did — it bought AMC stock itself, then issued derivative securities on-chain representing that stock and sold them to overseas investors, effectively "making its own share of AMC." AMC's Adam Aaron was unhappy, and Vlad Tenev asked "what's the problem?"

31:35 Apollo pays 100 basis points for its "aggressive" reputation
A paper measures private equity sponsors' reputations in three ways: having ChatGPT and Claude rank the most aggressive PE firms; looking at who has done liability management exercises (quasi-forced debt swaps); and putting Apollo in one bucket by itself and the other 24 firms in another. The conclusion: the most aggressive sponsors' portfolio companies borrow at noticeably higher yields, Apollo's loans are about 100 basis points more expensive than other sponsors', and the sample's average yield is 717 basis points. Matt calls it the "jerk premium" or the "aggression premium" — creditors expect to be squeezed, so they charge upfront.

item.title: The foldable phone isn't the future of phones — it's a two-in-one for a subset of people
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-cn1b5ef7-折叠屏不是手机的未来-是给一部分人的二合一/

item.description: Foldables have sold into the tens of millions, but the inner screen gets opened less than 30% of the time. They won't replace the slab phone; for people who want a phone-plus-iPad two-in-one they're a plus, and for everyone else they're a minus — you give up grip and performance.
item.content:encoded:
Foldables have sold into the tens of millions, but the inner screen gets opened less than 30% of the time. They won't replace the slab phone; for people who want a phone-plus-iPad two-in-one they're a plus, and for everyone else they're a minus — you give up grip and performance.

A solo episode with a product manager's lens that covers the real experience of using a foldable, the business logic behind Apple entering, and the judgment that phone form factors will diverge rather than converge. Medium information density; the back half is worth more than the front half.

12:17 The foldable's home turf is China and nowhere else
In 2025, China's full-year foldable shipments broke ten million units, with Huawei taking 70% — a crushing share. But globally, China is the largest single market, accounting for more than 40% of shipments. In other words, this category isn't evenly distributed the way other phone form factors are; its core user is the Chinese boss holding a Huawei foldable in first class and at social occasions. From the big picture, foldables are only 2.5% of global phone shipments, and only 15% of Huawei's own phone shipments.

20:23 The inner screen gets opened less than 30% of the time
Liu Fei used foldables as his daily driver for over half a month, and in the end he didn't want to keep them. The biggest problem wasn't the crease, the camera, or the battery — it was the scenario. The inner screen doesn't get opened much: it's unstable in one hand and prone to shaking, and it's more for two-handed use — but in that scenario he'd already be carrying a 10-inch iPad. A Vivo vice president said at a launch event that foldables keep getting better, but the core way they're used is no different from seven years ago, and many users open the inner screen less than 30% of the time. His analogy: it's like carrying a phone case with a built-in power bank — your phone's weight goes up permanently, but most of the time you don't need to charge, so you'd be better off carrying a separate external power bank.

23:25 Widening makes scrolling feeds worse, not better
To accommodate the outer screen, wide-fold designs like the Huawei Pure X Max and the Apple iPhone Door got wider, and scrolling feeds on them is terrible. Xiaohongshu is fine because it's been adapted; but when scrolling Meituan to filter restaurants or Taobao to filter shops, the information that fits on each screen suddenly shrinks. This isn't purely an adaptation problem, it's an aspect-ratio problem: list feeds run vertically, so widening is meaningless — height shrinks, and you see less at once. He recalls that ordering takeout on Meituan, he could only see three restaurants at a time.

29:33 Area grows 76%, but widescreen video actually gets smaller
A large foldable is nearly square when unfolded, which is a disaster for video and photos. By screen area, opening the inner screen adds 76%, nearly double; but if you're watching a widescreen movie, the foldable's inner screen actually loses about 10% of effective area, because it can't fit it. Watching 16:9 content does get bigger, but only by 20%, which is fairly limited. Wide-fold dimensions are more reasonable and the effective area is higher, but a 16:10 wide-fold playing 16:9 video still has about 10% black bars top and bottom. The point isn't that area naturally grows — it's what you actually want to do with the inner screen.

37:38 Who the two-in-one is a plus for
Liu Fei says the most important decision logic for whether to buy a foldable is: does it add to or subtract from your existing experience? He has a full set of devices himself — a Windows PC for gaming, a MacBook for work, an iPad for shows — so a foldable is pointless for him. But for many young people, the phone is their only computing device, and a lot of work gets done on the phone, offline; a bigger screen makes the experience much better. Salespeople who travel often and need to present a deck to a client in a café also get a much better result from the inner screen than the outer one. Flip it around: what you're buying isn't a slab phone that turns into a tablet, it's a foldable iPad mini.

45:47 Without AirPods there'd be no Chinese podcasting
Liu Fei says the Apple Watch and AirPods developed during Cook's tenure are both world-changing products, and AirPods especially so: without AirPods ushering in the era of Bluetooth noise-cancelling headphones, you could say there'd be no podcast market — especially no Chinese podcast market. Chinese podcasting took off in sync with Bluetooth noise-cancelling headphones — because with noise cancelling, you can actually hear what people are saying while commuting, working out, or doing chores. Before that, those scenarios were usually for listening to music, or to content with very low information density.

57:04 Apple's kill shot is migrating the iPad ecosystem
The iPhone Door doesn't have such an overwhelming hardware advantage; it uses materials from mature supply chains, weighs 254 grams, and doesn't feel dramatically different from Android flagship foldables. The core advantage is that Apple has the iPad: since the iPad launched in 2010, its 4:3 ratio has accumulated an enormous content ecosystem, and many apps were already optimised well enough for that ratio before foldable phones even existed, so they can be ported straight to the iPhone Door. For Android, that's a crushing level of ecosystem migration. Apple also did a lot of optimisation on one-handed interaction, putting frequently used buttons on the dominant-hand side — that's a system-level design, and it's relatively easy for developers to follow and adapt to.

1:08:09 How you define success decides whether it succeeds
Whether the iPhone Door succeeds depends on how you define success. If you define it as replacing the slab phone, it's nearly impossible; if you define it as becoming a product line that keeps selling, it's very possible. A few million units in the first generation is no problem, and it could even push toward ten million — JD.com reservations have already passed 500,000. Liu Fei says phone form factors won't converge, they'll diverge: the slab phone is the only form factor the whole world would vote for, but other form factors will keep existing and keep differentiating, at every price point and in every shape. Foldables won't replace slab phones, even if performance, experience and price were exactly the same, because a substantial number of people simply have no need to open the inner screen.

item.title: Americans Suddenly Love Japan, Not Because It's Cheap, But Because It's Normal

item.description: The real driver of Japan's tourism boom isn't the exchange rate, it's the functionality of public space—clean subways, on time, no trash. What American visitors experience in Tokyo is a society where entropy has been paused.
item.content:encoded:
The real driver of Japan's tourism boom isn't the exchange rate, it's the functionality of public space—clean subways, on time, no trash. What American visitors experience in Tokyo is a society where entropy has been paused.

This episode uses expert interviews and a listener survey to break down "why everyone's going to Japan" into six verifiable reasons. The second half, contrasting Japanese craft culture with American dysfunction, is especially worth hearing.

1:05 An Excel sheet of 119 visitors
The questioner, Lisa, is a Japanese person living in Tokyo. She made a visitor calendar from November 2022 to April 2026, with green cells marking when someone visited. She counted 119 people, 96 of them her own guests, averaging one person every five days, or 20% of all her days. She says she spends all her free time helping visiting friends plan their trips. This data visualization is itself evidence that the problem has spiraled out of control, and it's the starting point for the question this episode sets out to answer.

8:34 Japan is poor in resources, rich in story
Roland Kelts argues that the first reason for American interest in Japan isn't economic, it's story. He says Japan has almost no natural resources, no oil, very little land, only small rice paddies, but an astonishing culture of story. The world's first novel is Japanese, The Tale of Genji, a thousand years old. Through manga, anime, and the internet, the world discovered this narrative capacity. This didn't start in the 1990s; Roland says there were two earlier waves: Japanism in late 19th-century Europe, and the Beats' and hippies' fascination with Zen and Buddhist concepts in the 1950s and 60s.

15:05 America used to fear Japan
David Marks points out that for seventy years after World War II, mainstream America viewed Japan with fear, not affection. Before 1945 Japan was an enemy nation; afterward it was seen as a developing country rebuilding itself. In the 70s and 80s it became anxiety about Japan's economic power, with Michael Crichton's Rising Sun casting Japan as the villain. After the Cold War ended, there was even a CIA position paper discussing whether Japan should be the next enemy. When Japan's economic bubble burst in the 90s, America felt a sense of relief. When David moved to Japan in 2003, having a friend visit Japan was the event of the year, because nobody came.

24:29 The government made Japan cheap by design
The third wave was a government plan. In 2003, Junichiro Koizumi launched the Visit Japan campaign, aiming to raise the number of annual visitors from 5 million to 10 million, with ads full of Western stereotypes: geisha, cherry blossoms, temples. But what really worked was Shinzo Abe deliberately weakening the yen in the 2010s, originally to help exports, which ended up making hotels and restaurants cheap for foreigners. Roland says you can eat a very good soba lunch in Tokyo for under $10, while in New York $10 won't even buy you an apple and a banana. In 2013 Abe relaxed visas for Thailand and Malaysia, then China and Indonesia; Asian tourists surged first, followed by European and American tourists.

29:37 Japan's functionality is the biggest draw
Roland says the most important reason is functionality. Public spaces in many countries, especially the US, have become dysfunctional: parks are dirty and dangerous, rail systems are terrible, airports are a mess. In Japan, things just work. PJ adds that American ears hear complaints about poor public order and dirty subways as elitist, as rich people's complaints. But in Japan, wanting a clean subway isn't elitism—it's the opposite: why shouldn't public things be good? On Tokyo streets you see no trash, not even cigarette butts, and you don't smell urine or feces. PJ says this isn't the reason for a first visit, but it might be the reason some people go again.

36:52 Japan reveres makers, not sellers
The sixth reason is craft. The Japanese word shokunin refers to an artisan, someone who can make things extremely well. Such people are still respected in Japan, a tradition dating back to the 17th-century Edo period, when makers held higher status than merchants. Roland tells of an animation industry person explaining the Walmart model to him: in America, the company selling the goods comes first, nobody cares who made it, a $5 pillow was made by someone who knows nothing about pillows. But in Japan, the person who makes a pillow extremely well is the most valued. He took an American friend to a ramen shop, where they bought tickets and the ticket said come back at 3 p.m. After eating, the friend said it was the best soup of his life, then asked why they don't franchise. Roland said because franchising would mean losing control over the quality of the noodles, scallions, pork bone broth, and bamboo shoots—their scallions come from a man named Sato in Chiba who's been doing it for years.

41:10 Listener survey and experts almost perfectly overlap
Search Engine sent a questionnaire to hundreds of thousands of listeners and received a huge number of replies. Nearly half mentioned culture; some said they'd binge-watched anime since childhood, played Nintendo and Sony, were fans of Pokemon and One Piece. About a quarter mentioned the weak yen; one said the exchange rate was the best in 30 years. Others mentioned craft. What delighted PJ most were the reasons only a big survey could capture: someone decided to go because of FOMO after seeing so many people go, someone went to see the Godzilla museum—Godzilla brought in five listeners. And one-on-one stories: someone went to Japan to see the work of legendary bonsai master Mazuhiko Kimura; someone fell in love at 18, lost touch over a decade later, and the only way to see that person again was to fly to Japan, where they ended up spending four magical days in Osaka.

44:14 Japan is a place where entropy has been paused
Listeners' enthusiasm for functionality exceeded PJ's expectations. One said they took their family to Japan to show them what a high-functioning society actually looks like, everything on time, perfectly clean. One said public toilets are everywhere, with bidet functions, because everyone has to poop, and poop on your butt is disgusting. One said if every country respected each other like Japanese people do with their punctuality and queuing, the world would be much better. PJ himself says he still loves America, loves that anarchic mix, but feels something broke ten years ago—not just politics. Drivers are angrier, people are angrier, elbows are sharper, more people watch TikTok on the subway without headphones. He says America is like an eccentric friend who turned from quirky to not-so-good, which makes Japan's appeal understandable.
